articles.title: Sara Duterte: Prosecution in impeachment trial inventing evidence
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte criticized the prosecution on Monday in her impeachment trial, accusing it of fabricating evidence and claiming the cases against her are falling apart.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte criticized the prosecution on Monday in her impeachment trial, accusing it of fabricating evidence and claiming the cases against her are falling apart.

Duterte said this after the prosecution on Friday presented a forensic financial analyst who said that she and her husband, Atty. Manases "Mans" Carpio, had unexplained wealth and undeclared assets from 2022 to 2025 worth over P817 million.
A witness from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) also testified last week that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Carpio, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
Transaction records from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) showed that an estimated P4.4 billion went in and out of Carpio’s accounts from 2007 to 2025.

“Bumabagsak na yung kaso nila kaya binibilisan, kasi wala na silang masabi. Nag-iimbento ka ng ebidensya eh. Sa simula pa lang, yung impeachment complaint mo walang annexes, walang attached pieces of evidence,” Duterte told reporters.

(Their case is falling apart, so they are rushing things because they have nothing more to say. You’re making up evidence. From the very beginning, your impeachment complaint had no annexes or attached pieces of evidence.)
“Tapos gumawa ka, nag-imbento ka ng ebidensya. Sinubukan nila yun kay Madriaga. Bumagsak na yung bribery. Ngayon, sinubukan nila yung Grasioso. Wala na eh, bumagsak na," she added.
"Nagsisinungaling, nag-iimbento, kaya bumabagsak yung kaso, kaya nag-shift na yung narrative to China naman tayo ngayon,” she added.

(Then you made up evidence. They tried that with Madriaga, but the bribery allegation fell apart. Now they tried it with Gracioso, but that has also fallen apart. They are lying and fabricating evidence, which is why their case keeps falling apart. That is why they have now shifted the narrative to China.)
Duterte’s defense team maintained that there is no proof directly linking millions of pesos in her and her husband’s bank accounts to funds from the Chinese government.
AMLC records also did not show that China, as a country, funneled funds to Cale88.
The defense team also asserted that having recorded transactions does not automatically mean the money went directly to the Vice President and her husband.
In response, Duterte questioned the allegations and asked if doing business with China is prohibited.
"So ano ba talaga? Bawal ba talaga ang negosyo with China kasi it is a national security risk," Duterte said.

"Parang nakakahiya na nga yung drug haul na papuntang Pilipinas galing Laos and Thailand, tapos eto pa tayo na nagsasabing na naku, it’s a national security risk na mag-negosyo with China. Nagiging troublemaker of Southeast Asia tayo," she added.

(So what is it, then? Is doing business with China really prohibited because it poses a national security risk? It’s already embarrassing that we have a drug shipment bound for the Philippines from Laos and Thailand, and now we’re saying that doing business with China is a national security risk. We’re becoming the troublemaker of Southeast Asia.)
"Lahat na ay ginagawa ko kuno at lahat din ay gagawin din nila para pabagsakin ako because this is about the 2028 elections," he added.
(They claim that I’m doing all these things, and they will do everything they can to bring me down because this is all about the 2028 elections.)
The Senate Impeachment Court is currently tackling Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on the unexplained wealth of the Vice President.

In a Sunday Super Radyo dzBB interview, House prosecution panel member and Bukidnon Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores said they dropped the bribery charges against the Vice President to meet its timetable for presenting evidence.

“The only reason is the timetable. That’s really what we’re looking at. We want to finish this week because we’re about to go on a one-month break. We want the defense to begin after the break so the proceedings can continue smoothly,” Flores said.

“So far, we believe the other articles have been sufficiently established and can stand on their own without the bribery article having to be tried before the impeachment court,” he added. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] When power is inherited, who holds it accountable?
articles.summary: Those seeking power must accept scrutiny of their wealth, donors, interests and decisions. Every official owes the people accountability.

items: Democracy is threatened when citizens are held accountable for their earnings while public officials evade scrutiny regarding their wealth, highlighting the need for transparency and accountability in governance.

The article advocates for seven reforms to combat corruption, including modernizing revenue administration, verifying wealth, separating campaign financing from contracting, and enacting an anti-political dynasty law.

It emphasizes that public office should be treated as a public trust, requiring officials to be accountable for their wealth and decisions, and calls for a collaborative approach among government agencies to address unexplained wealth and corruption.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
A democracy is in danger when citizens must account for every peso they earn while those who spend public money treat questions about their wealth as “politicking.”

My recent interview about corruption inside the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) raised a question that reaches beyond the Philippines: Can government enforce accountability when the people exercising power are related to those entrusted to scrutinize them?

blocks.caption: [Ask the Tax Whiz] When power is inherited, who holds it accountable?

blocks.text: Congress must investigate abusive BIR audits. But intervention to shield family businesses or campaign donors from legitimate examination would turn oversight into protection. (See related articles below on BIR audits.)

Part 1 | [Ask the Tax Whiz] Why is the BIR auditing your business?Part 2 | [Ask the Tax Whiz] The BIR sent an audit notice. What now?Part 3 | [Ask the Tax Whiz] Will the new audit rules protect honest taxpayers?

“Privileged, entitled and convicted” should provoke scrutiny—not become politically acceptable credentials. These descriptions do not apply to every politician. But inherited influence cannot establish competence, and popularity cannot erase proven wrongdoing.

Before entrusting public money to someone without a documented employment or business record, ask how that person acquired their wealth and whether applicable taxes were paid. Claims that someone “never worked” or “never paid taxes” require evidence. So does any satisfactory explanation of materially unexplained wealth.
In my book, Reimagining the World: Without Corruption, I examine the relationship between wealth and power. Lord Acton warned: “Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.”
Consider the institutional risks.
The 20th Congress opened with four sibling pairs occupying one-third of the Senate: the Cayetanos, Tulfos, Villars, and half-brothers Jinggoy Estrada and JV Ejercito.

Former House speaker Martin Romualdez served in the House alongside his wife, Yedda, and son, Andrew Julian, both Tingog representatives. His first cousin, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., heads the executive branch, while the President’s son, Sandro, also serves in the House. Kinship does not prove corruption. It makes independent checks indispensable.

blocks.caption: How the Romualdezes held their political grip on Leyte for generations

blocks.text: In Samar, Rappler’s 2025 reporting documented Tan family members holding the governorship, vice governorship and both congressional seats. The Philippine Statistics Authority estimated that 24.9% of Samar’s families were poor in 2023.

In Davao City, Duterte family members won multiple executive and legislative positions in 2025; poverty affected 12.3% of its population in 2023. These figures use different measures and cannot be directly ranked or treated as proof of causation. They do, however, challenge the assumption that entrenched leadership guarantees shared prosperity.

blocks.caption: The Dutertes’ 40-year reign: Forged from strongman and victim

blocks.text: Luxury cars, condominiums and foreign travel do not, by themselves, prove criminality. But material discrepancies between spending and documented lawful resources warrant investigation. “Family money” cannot end the inquiry. Tax authorities should follow the money and pursue lawful remedies, including the principle often associated with the Al Capone case: when direct proof of a broader offense is difficult, tax violations may still establish accountability.

Neither can disaster publicity. Where evidence establishes responsibility for ghost flood-control projects, distributing relief cannot extinguish accountability—especially when there appear to be more cameras than supplies inside the relief bags.
A relief photograph cannot substitute for functioning infrastructure—or explain where its budget went.
Seven reforms would turn outrage into policy.

First, modernize revenue administration and protect its professionals. Give the BIR and Bureau of Customs greater fiscal and operational autonomy, with accountability and safeguards against political interference. Record political communications concerning individual audits and independently investigate improper pressure.

Autonomy must include investment in people. A compensation framework comparable in ambition to that of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas should provide financial security, professional fulfillment and credible careers. I propose remuneration substantially above relevant market benchmarks for highly qualified revenue professionals, matched by stricter recruitment, training, integrity checks and sanctions. Reward accurate assessments and fair treatment—not collections at any cost.

Second, verify wealth. Reform bank-secrecy restrictions for authorized investigations and require legally effective financial-access waivers from candidates and officials, subject to appropriate safeguards. Apply risk-based scrutiny to unexplained assets, gifts and inheritances. (READ: [Puso at Diwa] When AMLC’s financial intelligence speaks)

Third, separate campaign financing from contracting. Disclose donors and beneficial owners. Enact clear contracting restrictions covering donors, officials’ family businesses and proxies within the beneficiary official’s authority or influence.

Fourth, expand independent enterprise. Reserve 20% of local procurement value for qualified local micro, small and medium enterprises unaffiliated with officials or covered relatives. Give independent MSMEs with at least two years of operations priority opportunities in national procurement while preserving competition and quality.
Fifth, follow every payment. Require cashless contract payments linked to verified accounts, invoices, subcontractors and confirmed deliveries.

Sixth, make transparency operational. Advance CADENA’s budget-transparency objectives, complemented by appropriate blockchain applications, artificial-intelligence monitoring and independent inspections. Technology cannot certify an imaginary project.

Seventh, enact a genuine anti-political dynasty law. Congress must fulfill the constitutional duty affirmed by the Supreme Court to prohibit political dynasties through legislation. The law should meaningfully address both simultaneous control of public offices and succession designed to preserve family dominance. It needs clear coverage, enforceable disqualifications and safeguards against circumvention—not loopholes that protect the very arrangements it supposedly prohibits.
A law against political dynasties must actually disperse power.

blocks.caption: Why the SC is telling Congress to do its job on political dynasties

blocks.text: I urge the BIR to launch a nationwide, risk-based audit of unexplained wealth, starting with credible red flags involving political dynasties, their families, donors and contractors. Follow the money and prosecute tax evasion wherever the evidence leads—including cases linked to corruption, smuggling and money laundering. Strengthen the law to permanently bar convicted tax evaders from elected or appointed public office. No surname should shield wrongdoing. No public office should shelter it.

Leave compliant MSMEs, registered business enterprises, online sellers and content creators free to build their businesses. Audit them when credible information or material tax risks justify examination—not simply because they are visible, accessible or easier to pressure.
Enforcement should follow the risk, not the easiest taxpayer to audit.

Start with a group chat, if that is what it takes to get the agencies talking: BIR, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, Bureau of Customs, Securities and Exchange Commission, Land Registration Authority and Ombudsman. Then turn that conversation into a formal inter-agency mechanism with designated investigators, secure and lawful information sharing, documented referrals and clear deadlines. Confidential records belong in protected systems, not informal chats.

The objective is straightforward: connect income, ownership, property, financial intelligence and public-accountability records so that unexplained wealth does not remain unexplained simply because agencies work in isolation.
For investors, reform means fairer competition. For citizens, it means healthcare, education and infrastructure delivered without political indebtedness.
Fighting corruption is fighting poverty when it protects resources and opportunity.
Public office is a public trust—not a family business.
Those seeking power must accept scrutiny of their wealth, donors, interests and decisions. The people owe no dynasty a political future. Every official owes the people accountability.
Our children deserve to inherit a country of opportunity—not a government already reserved for someone else’s children. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard), is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal). He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon batters Mexico's Pacific Coast
articles.summary: Hurricane Simon is currently running parallel to Mexico's Pacific Coast, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds to vulnerable towns.

image.caption: Authorities have established emergency shelters for those affected by the hurricaneImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hurricane Simon lashed vulnerable resorts and towns along Mexico's Pacific Coast on Sunday as it moved parallel to the shoreline, despite weakening to a category 3 storm.
"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the US National Hurricane Center's advisory said.
Simon is expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back towards Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it said.
On high alert

Mexican authorities have placed 28 municipalities across the states of Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level. Another 93 municipalities were under high ‌alert, according to civil protection bulletins.

blocks.caption: Strong winds are battering the coastal states on the Pacific end of MexicoImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: The hurricane's center closed in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rains were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in Jalisco. Apart from the resorts, several Mexicans live in communities inland and uphill, in houses that may not be able to weather the storm.
How to protect houses from natural disasters
Experts believe the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

blocks.caption: heavy rainfall overnight has increased the risk of flooding and muslidesImage: Daniel Becerril/REUTERS

blocks.text: In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped rescue locals from the overnight rainfall.
"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.
How do tropical storms form?
"My mother doesn't want ‌to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but ‌she doesn't ​want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."
Airport closed, authorities urge caution
Puerto Vallarta International Airport was closed temporarily while authorities suspended non-essential activities.
They also established emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.
Earlier on Sunday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors ahead of the storm.
Hurricane Simon has come days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, knocking down power lines and flooding the streets.

articles.title: Doctor warned Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home years before religious sect killed her by withdrawing medicine
articles.summary:
Coronial inquest begins into death of eight-year-old after 14 members of Toowoomba sect the Saints, including her parents, were found guilty of her manslaughter

  • Get our

blocks.text: A medical specialist at the Queensland Children’s hospital warned that Elizabeth Struhs would not be safe at home with her mother years before her parents allowed her to die by withdrawing lifesaving medicine, a coronial inquest has heard.

Elizabeth, a type 1 diabetic, died at the age of eight from diabetic ketoacidosis on 7 January 2022, at her family home in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, after her parents and other members of a religious sect withdrew the insulin she needed to survive and sat around singing and praying while she slowly died over the course of several days.

All 14 adult members of the sect, known as the Saints, were convicted of her manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, mother, Kerrie Struhs, and brother, Zachary Struhs, and the leader of their sect, Brendan Stevens.
The group, which some have referred to as “a cult”, did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her incurable illness and be resurrected after she died.

Elizabeth had been hospitalised in 2019 in a similar incident. Her mother, Kerrie, openly refused to provide her medical care and was charged and convicted with failing to provide her the necessaries of life as a result of the incident in 2021.
A coronial inquest, which sat for its first day on Monday, heard that doctors had attempted to warn the child safety department that Elizabeth could not be safely returned to Kerrie.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard heard from an experienced medical specialist who helped care for Elizabeth after her admission to the Queensland children’s hospital’s intensive care unit on 17 July 2019. The doctor cannot be identified for legal reasons.
The doctor wrote a professional report about the child one day later raising concerns about her safety, the inquest heard.
The doctor said she was concerned partly due to Elizabeth’s condition at presentation, describing her as “extremely unwell” and requiring intubation and a ventilator.
But she was also concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth’s mother, Kerrie, she said.
Kerrie refused to even attend the hospital to see her child, and denied that she was sick or would ever require medication in a phone conversation, the doctor told the court.
Kerrie also had no questions about her daughter’s condition, the doctor said.
Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris read from the doctor’s nine-page report, which was sent to child safety and the police.
“‘Type 1 diabetes is a life-threatening condition that requires complicated care by the parents, the report reads,” he said.
“If her mother continues to deny the requirement for insulin and the related treatments Elizabeth could not be in Kerrie’s care’.
“With ‘not’ in bold,” Hamlyn-Harris added.
The doctor consulted the hospital’s child protection and forensic medical service before writing the report.
after newsletter promotion
“My concerns were so strong that if [a nurse at the service] had said not to I was still planning to submit a report,” the doctor said.

Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary, intensive arrangement which allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard.
The court heard this was done without the knowledge of the hospital team.
“There is still significant risk in that context,” the doctor said, on Monday.
“I would not be supportive of that treatment if I was the clinician involved in that discharge home plan.”
The doctor said she raised concerns at the time that diabetes required lifelong treatment, and that the risk posed by the illness can change over time, due to physical or social changes.
Elizabeth’s father, Jason, agreed to care for Elizabeth after her discharge from hospital, which he did for three years.

At the time, Jason was a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, and had saved Elizabeth’s life by taking her to hospital against the wishes of his wife in 2019 and then testified against her at a criminal trial.

Both Jason and Kerrie were found guilty in 2021 of failing to supply the necessaries of life for their daughter, relating to the incident in 2019 which was so serious Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a coma.

Jason was sentenced to six months in prison, wholly suspended for a period of 12 months, while Kerrie was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment with a specified parole release date of 15 December 2021.
But Kerrie helped convert Jason to her religious beliefs while serving her prison sentence. He was then convinced to give up treating Elizabeth’s diabetes with insulin, leading to her death.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Defense cites penalties for confidentiality breach; witness says he's not scared
articles.summary: Financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera, a witness presented by the prosecution, said Monday he is not scared even as Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer read a provision of the law amending…

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published October 12, 2026 2:30pm

Financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera, a witness presented by the prosecution, said Monday he is not scared even as Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer read a provision of the law amending the Anti-Money Laundering Act, pertaining to the penalties for the breach of confidentiality.
On Day 38 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Ferrer cited Section 9(d) of Republic Act No. 9194, which provided the penalties for malicious reporting under the AMLA.
“Letter D, Breach of Confidentiality. I will no longer specify the penalties, but it includes imprisonment and fine. But it is not meant to scare you, sir,” the defense lawyer said.
Cabrera answered, “I’m not scared naman po.”

Section 9(d) of RA 9194 states that: The punishment of imprisonment ranging from three to eight years and a fine of not less than P500,000, but not more than P1,000,000, shall be imposed on a person convicted for a violation under the law.
In the case of a breach of confidentiality that is published or reported by the media, the responsible reporter, writer, president, publisher, manager and editor-in-chief shall be held liable.

Ferrer then asked the witness if, as a lawyer, he did not feel concerned that the furnishing of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) documents to him by the prosecution without the permission of the Senate impeachment court may violate such laws.
“Dahil na-take up na po sa House, at pinagtalunan na po sa House, kaya po ang nasa isip ko ay ay okay lang po ‘yun na tanggapin ko,” Cabrera said.
(Since these have already been taken up and debated in the House of Representatives, I felt it was okay for me to accept these.)
When the trial resumed on Monday morning, Ferrer and Cabrera also shared a light moment when the latter called the defense lawyer, “Honorable Kristine,” when he greeted her good morning.
“Just don’t call me Honorable because I’m not an Honorable…I’m not part of the prosecution team,” Ferrer said.
Cabrera is testifying for Article 2 of the impeachment case, which accuses the Vice President of amassing unexplained wealth.
He is the last witness that would be presented by the prosecution in the impeachment trial. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecution won't seek Sara Duterte as hostile witness anymore
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel said Monday it will no longer be seeking to field Vice President Sara Duterte as a hostile witness in her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 2:22pm
The House prosecution panel said Monday it will no longer be seeking to field Vice President Sara Duterte as a hostile witness in her impeachment trial.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said that given that the previous hostile witness from the Office of the Vice President merely said they do not know or were unaware of the allegations, it is likely that the Vice President will do the same.

“From everything we have heard from the defense, she is just going to say, hindi ko alam. That is all she is going to say on the witness stand. She is not going to enlighten the senator-judges, nor the public for her accountability of public funds, unexplained wealth, and grave threats to the President, First Lady, and former Speaker,” Kapunan said.
(She will just say she doesn't know)

“It will be good for the prosecution [if she takes the witness stand]. Makikita natin iyong init ng ulo niya, ang pagkalutang niya (We can see her hotheadedness), but it will be an absolute waste of the prosecution’s time when the testimony is predictable,” she added.

Kapunan and her fellow private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. also noted that calling Duterte as a witness remains an option for the defense, and the prosecution can take a crack at cross-examining her just the same.
“The defense would have a better control of her on what she would say and how to behave,” she said.
"If you want to present the Vice President, please, do so. I am dying to cross examine her. I volunteer [to do it]," Kapunan added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Pulse Asia: Grace Poe, Alan Cayetano top senatorial preferences for May 2028 polls
articles.summary: Former senator Grace Poe and Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano emerged as the most preferred senatorial candidates among Filipino adults for the May 2028 elections, according to the latest…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 2:13pm

Former senator Grace Poe and Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano emerged as the most preferred senatorial candidates among Filipino adults for the May 2028 elections, according to the latest survey by Pulse Asia.
In the survey conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026, 15 candidates emerged as probable winners among the 66 individuals included in the senatorial preference poll.
Most of those with a statistical chance of winning are either former or incumbent members of Congress, Pulse Asia said.
Poe led the list with 50.2%, placing her in a statistical ranking of first to second, followed by Cayetano with 46.5%, placing him first to fourth.
Senator Robin Padilla (45.9%) and Senator Raffy Tulfo (44.4%) shared the second to fourth places.
Other potential winners completing the top half of the list were Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte (37.2%), former senator Emmanuel “Manny” Pacquiao (36.5%) and Senator Loren Legarda (33%).

Rounding out the 15 probable winners were Makati City Mayor Nancy Binay, Senator Francis "Chiz" Escudero, Education Secretary Sonny Angara, media personality Ben Tulfo, Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (Tieza) head Mark Lapid, detained Senator Jinggoy Estrada, showbiz celebrity Willie Revillame and former AnaKalusugan party-list Rep. Mike Defensor.
Meanwhile, 3.6% of respondents had yet to decide on their senatorial preferences, while 2.8% said they would not support any of the possible candidates. Another 0.9% declined to state their opinion.
Pulse Asia interviewed 2,400 representative adults nationwide face-to-face for the survey. The survey had a margin of error of ±2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.

For results in each of the four areas covered by the survey — Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao — the margin of error was ±4 percentage points, meaning the actual figures could be 4 points higher or lower than the survey results. —MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Mystery of 1950s wedding photo album found dumped in Wakefield solved
articles.summary:
Online appeal and detective work by local historian help to return keepsake to couple’s sone after it had been stolen

When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album…

blocks.text: When Andrew Bedford discovered an old wedding album dumped outside his city centre cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, he considered chucking it into a nearby wheelie bin.
But when he opened the album, the vintage photographs of the happy couple on their wedding day in 1957 seemed too precious to throw away.
Unable to work out the identity of the bride and groom – their handwritten names had become too faded to read – he rescued the album and brought it back to his cafe, Eva’s Kitchen, for safekeeping.
His partner, Éva Lemperger, put out a plea on social media to help identify the couple.
Now the mystery has been solved after a local family historian took up the case and tracked down the couple’s 65-year-old son, Michael Dawson.
He revealed the album had been stolen from a storage unit near the cafe, along with other cherished family heirlooms, after his parents died.
It contains some of his only surviving photographs of his mother and father, Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr, and he now plans to “protect it with [his] life”.

blocks.caption: The wedding photos were found to be of Maxwell Dawson and Barbara Parr. Photograph: Andrew Bedford

blocks.text: Bedford said: “I was just so happy he got it back. I thought, if it had been mine, and I’d lost pictures of my family – and they were only pictures I had of them – I’d have been elated if somebody had found them and given them back to me.”

When the case of the mysterious wedding album was picked up by his local newspaper, the Wakefield Express, it caught the attention of a local historian and amateur sleuth, Anne-Marie Fawcett. “I run a local history group on Facebook with over 15,000 members, and I’m really interested in local history, particularly family history,” she said.

“I love researching. I love uncovering stories and finding connections. And I like getting to the bottom of mysteries … When I saw that nobody knew who the album belonged to, I thought, that’s something to get my teeth into.”

A clue in the birth certificate of another guest helped her to identify the church the couple were married in: Wadsley Parish Church in Sheffield. She then used a photo enhancing tool to decipher the name of the bride. “But there was more than one Barbara Parr in the records, so I had to follow them all.”

When she came across an electoral roll entry suggesting Parr’s husband, Maxwell, had lived near Wakefield, she guessed she had found the right couple and appealed for information about the family on social media.

blocks.caption: Eva’s Kitchen cafe in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. Photograph: Andrew Bedford

blocks.text: An old school friend of Michael Dawson’s remembered him and helped Fawcett to find a photograph of him, enabling her to track him down on Facebook.
“I sent him a message, and he rang me,” said Fawcett. “He was absolutely made up.”

Dawson told her the album had been stolen from the storage unit where he and his brother had stored the cherished contents of his parents’ home after they died. “Someone had broken in and taken all the family treasure. He said he’d lost everything. So you can imagine how I felt to be able to reunite him with this [album] … I’ve got goose pimples talking about it. Everybody loves a happy ending, don’t they?”
Dawson told the BBC: “I’m absolutely elated because I am sentimental and it’s important for me to have these photos.
“I will protect it with my life now, based on the fact that it’s all I’ve got.”
Asked how he felt about Fawcett’s detective efforts, he joked: “I think she probably knows more about me than I do, which is a worry.”
But he added: “I thought I’d lost everything. I can’t thank her enough.”

articles.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
articles.summary:
Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294

Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the…

blocks.text: Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.

The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia.

The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs.

The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption.
The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades.

Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.

The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA).

Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel.
“Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.”

Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group.
The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC.

“As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.”

Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said.

On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The government was contact for comment.

articles.title: Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
articles.summary:
Council car parks have switched away from ticket machines to cut costs, leading to extra fees for users

Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to…

blocks.text: Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab.

Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee.

Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”.

These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps.

Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased.

blocks.caption: For many motorists simply downloading a parking app and then going through the payment process itself is chore enough. Photograph: Simon Dack/Alamy

blocks.text: These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff.
Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff.
Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text.

According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle.
However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs.
Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged.
The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country.

RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked.

PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it.

Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset.

blocks.caption: Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines. Photograph: Howard_M/Getty Images/iStockphoto

blocks.text: MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex.

RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive.

JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.”

PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.”
MiPermit was contacted for a comment.
The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront.

The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for the AA said: “When a driver walks to the signs in the car park and sees £1 per hour, that’s what they should be charged, not £1 plus a 25p service charge.”

articles.title: Delhi police shut metro stations ahead of election protest march
articles.summary:
India’s opposition parties and supporters of the ‘cockroach’ youth movement have been demonstrating against a ⁠controversial revision of election voter ⁠lists

Authorities in India’s capital…

blocks.text: Authorities in India’s capital closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions on Monday, as opposition parties planned to march to the supreme court in protest against a ⁠controversial revision of voter ⁠lists that has sparked days ​of unrest in Delhi.

Opposition parties and supporters of the “cockroach” youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner ⁠Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – deleted from voter lists during a verification exercise, including 30 million who could not be traced. Others included 28 million people who had died, and 63 million who had relocated.

Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject.

Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders ​of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), as supporters of the youth movement ‌sought to march in protest and were ‌stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi.

The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.

blocks.caption: Security personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner on Sunday. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police said the six metro stations were closed on Monday for “security reasons” and traffic restrictions and diversions would be imposed in 20 locations.
The main opposition Congress party has announced a march to the supreme court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls “vote theft” and Kumar’s resignation.
“Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the ‌Constitution of India, will walk with us,” Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X.

Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined a meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the ​Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue was already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said.
Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi police to “demand” a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new call to protest if a date is not given within 24 hours.

The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months ⁠against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to ​Modi and his BJP in his 12 ​years in power.

The protests erupted after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, ​registration procedures and digital systems.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No special barangay, SK elections on November 28, 2026
articles.summary: Comelec debunked the circulating graphic as false and a manipulated version of the Batanes Lone Legislative District Special Election calendar of activities

blocks.text: Claim: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) released a calendar of activities for the special barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) on November 28, 2026.

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook page Rosas Marlon Vlogs posted the claim on October 5. The post included a graphic supposedly released by Comelec detailing the calendar of activities for the barangay and SK special elections, specifying dates for the start of certificate of candidacy filing, campaign period, and election day on November 28, 2026.
The original post was deleted. However, several accounts reposted the graphic.
One post by Jay-ar Arceño reached over 300 reactions and 100 comments as of writing. Kahzumie Izunah also posted the graphic, which reached 300 reactions and 100 shares.
The facts: There will be no special elections for barangay and SK positions on November 28, 2026. Comelec debunked the circulating claim in a Facebook post on October 8.
The commission flagged the graphic as a manipulated version of a calendar of activities for the special election in Batanes.

“Totoo ang magaganap na Special Elections sa Lone Legislative District ng Lalawigan ng Batanes sa November 28, 2026 para punan ang posisyong nabakante ng yumaong kongresista nito na si Hon. Ciriaco B. Gato, Jr.,” the statement read.

(The Special Election for the Lone Legislative District of the Province of Batanes will indeed take place on November 28, 2026, to fill the position vacated by its late congressman, Hon. Ciriaco B. Gato, Jr.)

However, the poll body clarified that there will be no special barangay and SK elections in the province of Batanes or anywhere else in the country. The commission warned social media users to be cautious with unverified information and reminded them to cross-check official statements from Comelec and other reliable sources.

BSKE postponement: On September 24, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12326, which fixes the term of barangay and SK officials to five years and postpones the BSKE slated in November 2026 to November 2028.
The law states that incumbent elective barangay officials would be considered to have completed one term in their respective positions, considering the extension of their terms by two years.
It also clarified that those serving their final term will be ineligible to run for the same position in the November 2028 BSKE.
The last BSKE was held in 2023, with the next one originally slated for December 2025 before Marcos signed a law moving the date to November 2026.
Earlier in September, the House of Representatives and the Senate passed their versions of the bill setting a five-year term for barangay and SK officials. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Cabrera says VP Sara, Mans Carpio financial docs used in report from prosecution
articles.summary: Financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera said Monday he did not use any documents coming from Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, when doing the report detailing…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 1:32pm

Financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera said Monday he did not use any documents coming from Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, when doing the report detailing findings on the couple’s financial records.
Cabrera made the confirmation during his cross-examination by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer on Day 38 of the trial.
“According to page 1 of your report, if you can refer to it, you did not examine or use any document coming from the respondent and her spouse. Correct?” Ferrer asked.
Cabrera tried to explain his answer but was stopped by the defense lawyer midway, asking him to simply answer the question.
“Wala po kasi, ‘yan po ‘yung sagot. Wala po kasi do’n sa reply, ‘yung answer niya sa House at saka sa Senate. Wala po kasi,” the witness said.
(There was none, that’s the answer. It’s not in the reply, in her answer to the House of Representatives and the Senate. There was nothing.)
Ferrer clarified if his answer means yes.
“Had there been, I would have used po,” Cabrera said.
Ferrer pressed Cabrera if the answer was yes, which the witness answered in the affirmative.
The defense lawyer also asked him if he did not interview Duterte, Carpio, their accountants and their auditors. Cabrera affirmed.

Based on Cabrera’s report, which was presented in the Senate impeachment court, documents that were analyzed involved Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) from 2022 to 2025; reports from the Anti–Money Laundering Council (AMLC); income tax returns filed by Duterte and Carpio; their bank statements and bank records; and the financial statements of corporations they have interest in, among others.
The witness noted he received bank documents from the prosecution beginning the second week of September.
He, however, said he does not recall seeing transmittal letters from the prosecution. He said he did not also give the prosecution a list of documents that he received.
During the trial on Friday, Cabrera revealed findings that Duterte and her husband supposedly had P817.87 million in allegedly undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

Cabrera said he had arrived at the number after piercing the corporate veil—a legal principle wherein the court overlooks the company's separate legal personality and directly holds the individuals responsible.

The financial analyst put together the Duterte-Carpio couple's undeclared cash, undeclared personal and other real properties, undeclared income, undeclared income from companies Cale88 and Metro City, and total undeclared income from Gencorp, from 2022 to 2025. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecution forgoes plan to ask VP Sara Duterte to testify in own trial
articles.summary: 'We don't see the need to get her testimony anymore, when the records, most of them which came from her, speak loudly,' prosecutor Jay Tolosa says

blocks.text: HOSTILE. Private prosecutor Jay Tolosa questions hostile witness, Atty. Michael Poa, during Day 21 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 2, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
'We don't see the need to get her testimony anymore, when the records, most of them which came from her, speak loudly,' prosecutor Jay Tolosa says

items: The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has decided not to call her as a witness, citing sufficient evidence from bank records and financial statements.
Prosecutors believe the evidence presented is strong enough without her testimony, while the defense argues that it is their strategy to call her if needed.
The prosecution is seeking Duterte's removal from office for various offenses, including betrayal of public trust and misuse of funds, but has dropped the bribery case to expedite the trial.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has dropped its earlier plan to call her to the witness stand.

The prosecution is expected to wrap up its case against the Vice President after the conclusion of the examination of its last witness, financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, on Monday, October 12.
Prosecution legal spokesman Jay Tolosa said the bank records and Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth of Duterte already suffice.

“Every time we make decisions about witness we will present, it’s always based on analysis of evidence we’ve presented so far. We’re already satisfied with the evidence that we presented, and the case that we built,” Tolosa said in a press conference.

“We don’t see the need to get her testimony anymore, when the records, most of them which came from her, speak loudly,” he added. “If the Vice President will just claim she had no knowledge, we don’t see the need to burden the court’s calendar and senator-judges with that kind of testimony.”

blocks.caption: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial

blocks.text: Prosecutor Joel Chua said it would be more appropriate for the defense team to call its own client to the witness stand.
“That could be their legal strategy, so the Vice President can explain the documents we presented,” Chua added.
Last month, the prosecution said it would ask the court to subpoena the Vice President after the presentation of all remaining impeachment articles.

“All of these pawns, and castles, and horses, and bishops point to only one person, and that accountable person is the Vice President,” private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan had argued, referring to the Duterte’s role at the time in the confidential funds mess involving the government agencies she has handled.
The defense team opposed the move, citing Article 3, Section 17 of the Constitution which states that “no person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”

“It is clear that respondent is here through her counsel. If respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her,” lead defense lawyer Sheila Sison had said.

The prosecution seeks Duterte’s removal from office for betrayal of public trust, culpable violation of the Constitution and other impeachable offenses related to her alleged misuse of funds, apparent grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., alleged unexplained wealth, and supposed bribery of government officials.
The prosecution has already dropped the bribery case in a bid to expedite the proceedings. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bong Go leads vice-presidential preference survey for May 2028 polls -- Pulse Asia
articles.summary: Senator Christopher “Bong” Go is the top choice among seven potential candidates for vice president in the May 2028 national elections, according to a Pulse Asia survey conducted from September 17 to…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 1:02pm

Senator Christopher “Bong” Go is the top choice among seven potential candidates for vice president in the May 2028 national elections, according to a Pulse Asia survey conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026.

Go led the vice-presidential preference survey, ahead of Senators Robin Padilla, Bam Aquino, Erwin Tulfo and Kiko Pangilinan, as well as former Senator Grace Poe and Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) General Manager Nicolas Torre III.
Go received the support of 31% of Filipino adults, with his highest ratings recorded in Mindanao (55%), the Visayas (37%), the upper-income Class ABC (37%) and the middle-income Class D (31%).
Following Go were Padilla with 19%, Aquino with 17%, Poe with 14%, Tulfo with 10%, Pangilinan with 3% and Torre with 0.3%.
Padilla's support was highest among the low-income (Class E) respondents at 40% and lowest among the upper-income (Class ABC) respondents at 7%.

Two percent of respondents were undecided about their choice for vice president in the May 2028 elections, while another 2% said they would not support any of the potential candidates. One percent declined to state their preference.

At the time of the survey, Padilla had been subpoenaed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) in connection with an obstruction of justice complaint filed against him over the departure of Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa from Senate premises amid reports of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant against him.
Pulse Asia said it interviewed 2,400 representative Filipino adults face-to-face for the survey. The survey reportedly had a margin of error of ±2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.

For subnational estimates, the margin of error was ±4 percentage points at the 95% confidence level for each of the following areas: Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao. — MCG, GMA News
