articles.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth
articles.summary: Backdated paperwork also made the Russian oligarch’s yachts and mansions disappear from accounts, BBC finds.
articles.byline: James Oliver, Rory Tinman, Simon Lock

blocks.text: The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".

Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.

For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.

Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.

Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

An email from MeritServus in August 2005 to Abramovich's Russian associates said a plan had been devised after a meeting with Deloitte. "If you agree, it will be necessary to change the financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004," the email read.
MeritServus informed the oligarch's Russian associates, that Kravin's "Provisional Tax Assessments for 2005" would be filed showing the company earning no income from the money.
A month later, an associate in Russia emailed in response, "I agree".
MeritServus then created a series of backdated documents which falsely purported to show that Kravin was only holding and investing the funds on behalf of its parent company in the BVI.
This made it look like Kravin did not actually own the money, so it would not be liable for tax in Cyprus.

Deloitte wrote in a September 2005 email that "certain changes will have to be made to the accounts (bank account balances, interest income, profit and loss account)" because of the backdated changes to Kravin's assets.
So Deloitte was apparently advising on the falsification of financial records. The evidence suggests it allowed Abramovich's company to evade millions in tax.

Andrew Mitchell KC told us the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion. "If it happened in England and it was in the millions, His Majesty's Revenue and Customs would be thinking about a prosecution," he said.

Cypriot MP Christos Christofides said that if tax had been evaded, then "we have to see how we can get our money back and how, if some people are guilty, they have to pay the price according to our law."

In addition to the documents which Deloitte helped to backdate, Abramovich's advisers at MeritServus falsified a third set of records. This involved the oligarch's huge business fortune - more than $10bn - held by a company called Electus Investments in Cyprus.
MeritServus backdated documents to make it look like Electus did not own the fortune.
It used another Abramovich company with exactly the same name of Electus Investments, but this time based in the more secretive BVI, where accounts did not have to be made public.

Emails show that in 2006, MeritServus acknowledged that the fortune was owned by Electus Cyprus. But again it proposed to rewrite the past, this time "to transfer the beneficial ownership to Electus Investments in the BVI" and make it look as though the change had happened three years earlier.

MeritServus signed and backdated documents which falsely purported to show the BVI company had owned the $10bn fortune since 20 November 2003. So when the accounts of the Cypriot company with the same name were made public, it appeared to have assets worth just $145,000.
Roman Abramovich's billions had been made to disappear.

articles.title: Met chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more black and Asian officers
articles.summary: Mark Rowley says inclusivity is crucial for the force and he refuses to be ‘blown off course’ by critics
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: Mark Rowley has said the Metropolitan police must recruit more black and Asian officers in order to gain the trust of minority ethnic communities in London, and vowed not to be “blown off course by the culture wars”.

The right has criticised drives for diversity, claiming they lead to lower standards. Rowley, who is commissioner of the Met and Britain’s top police officer, said that as a leader of a major organisation he was prepared to take a stand against the “toxicity” surrounding the diversity debate and criticised other leaders for “running away from the subject”.

In London, 46% of people are from a minority ethnic background, compared with 18% of Met officers. Rowley said he was driven by operational necessity, not politics, and believed “inclusivity” was vital to policing by consent, which is the philosophical cornerstone of British policing.

“We cannot police London effectively if we fail to recruit from all of London,” he writes in the Guardian. “Effective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent which stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.”
He writes: “Today, we are launching a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity.

“We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences. An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.”

blocks.caption: Police oversee a far-right Britain First march in Manchester last year. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rowley is braced for attacks from some on the left who may say his force is not going far enough, as well as from those on the right who are critical of diversity, equity and inclusivity (DEI) initiatives.

Many on the right have previously accused police of being “woke” and of “two-tier policing”, a claim that alleges people from ethnic minorities are favoured over white people, when the evidence shows the opposite.

“The toxicity is horrible around the DEI debate,” Rowley said. “Lots of leaders, both in the public and private sector, are running away from the subject. I think leaders need to stand up and make a practical case. We need to do what works for policing London.”

The Met is disproportionately white. It has the greatest number of black and Asian officers of any force in the UK, but also the biggest race gap – the difference between the ethnic makeup of its officers compared with the population it serves.
The gap is starkest with black officers, who make up 3.7% of the Met compared with 13.5% of London’s population overall.

Rowley writes that the barriers have lasted for generations and limited opportunities. “Some will wrongly argue that recruiting from under-represented communities means lowering standards. It does not and they are wrong,” he writes.

“Historically, some groups faced barriers that made it harder to join policing, harder to access specialist training and harder to progress into some roles. Removing those barriers is not favouritism, it is fairness.”
after newsletter promotion

The Met was found to be institutionally racist by the 1999 Macpherson inquiry into failings that meant it took 19 years for the killers of the black student Stephen Lawrence to be convicted of his murder.

In 2023, the Casey report, commissioned by the Met, found the force to be institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic. Rowley accepted the findings and said bias was systemic but rejected the label of “institutional”, believing it was politicised and ambiguous.
Louise Casey and others subsequently warned that Rowley would struggle to repair the poor trust levels among black people in London when it came to the police.

Last year, Met officers at Charing Cross police station ​were recorded calling for immigrants to be shot, bragging about excessive use of force, being dismissive about a rape complaint and making anti-Muslim and anti-women comments.

Responding to Rowley’s recruitment drive, Leroy Logan, who joined the Met in 1983 and was the first chair of the Met’s black police association, said he would hesitate to join the Met now. “The Met is seen as a safe haven for white supremacists. It has gone backwards since Macpherson,” he said.

“It has lacked the leadership and the culture,” Logan added. “My younger self would be really questioning whether to join now. The Met has not helped itself to ensure the experience of black people at the hands of the police is as fair and just as for white people. People are not going to join just because Sir Mark Rowley says so.”

articles.title: Burnham to urge MPs to embrace closer ties with EU
articles.summary:
Post-recess statement will focus on damage caused by Brexit and the need to cooperate on immigration and trade

Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from recess, warning that failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.

The prime minister will use a statement to the Commons on the first day back after the party conference break to urge MPs to face up to the damage caused by Brexit, and embrace closer ties with the EU to increase economic growth and tackle illegal immigration.

In a stern warning ahead of the upcoming UK-EU summit, Burnham will argue that Britain cannot afford to turn its back on opportunities for greater cooperation with Europe and that maintaining the status quo is no longer good enough.
He will call for a calm, clear-eyed assessment of Britain’s relationship with Europe and urge MPs from across the Commons to back a pragmatic approach.
Burnham is expected to argue that most of the public would expect the government to seize the opportunity if closer cooperation could strengthen immigration controls while reviving the economy.

A No 10 source said: “Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be.
“Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty.”
The prime minister’s statement comes on the same day MPs are due to debate a petition in Westminster Hall, calling for Britain to apply to rejoin the EU, which got more than 111,000 signatures.

The intervention comes amid renewed divisions over Britain’s relationship with Europe, with senior Conservatives vowing to reverse Labour’s moves towards closer EU ties, including a proposed agreement designed to ease post-Brexit barriers on food and agricultural trade. It has prompted warnings from businesses that abandoning such arrangements could prolong costs and uncertainty caused by checks and paperwork at the border.

But the idea of Britain having a closer relationship with the EU has also prompted unease within Burnham’s own ranks. Some MPs representing leave-voting constituencies fear renewing the Brexit debate could reopen old divisions, with senior ministers warning of the political and economic risks of pursuing EU membership.

Burnham’s statement also follows his declaration on Sunday that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. The prime minister has said he sought clarification on foreign interference after entering Downing Street and received confirmation of Russian involvement, although he did not reveal the evidence or suggest it had changed the referendum result.
after newsletter promotion
The prime minister has already signalled a significant change in tone from his predecessor Keir Starmer, who ruled out rejoining the single market or customs union.

At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done more harm than good and promised to examine Britain’s longterm relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc.

Monday’s statement will turn the focus towards the immediate negotiations, with ministers seeking progress on removing trade barriers, including bureaucracy affecting food imports and exports, and closer cooperation on migration.

articles.title: How Iran's elite forces 'mold the minds of the young cadets'
articles.summary: Months of correspondence with two high-ranking defectors have given DW's investigative unit a rare look at the mindset of the regime's loyal servants — and revealed a clandestine circle that…

image.caption: The two men gave DW insight into the workings of Iran's security forcesImage: DW

blocks.text: Omid, whose real name cannot be used, signed up to join Iran's security forces when he was 18 years old and harbored "a deep commitment to my country." At the academy, Omid told DW, cadets were under the regime's control "day and night," from their military training through the daily prayers and speeches.
"They mold the minds of the young cadets," Omid said.

Some of these recruits, Omid said, eventually rise through the ranks of Iran's security apparatus to join an elite cadre of officers who plot missions, abductions and assassinations inside and outside of Iran — and have access to unlimited resources and personnel. And, he said, he attended their meetings.

blocks.caption: "Omid" was a commander in Iran's special forces. Image: DW

blocks.text: A defector speaks

When Omid, a burly man who carries scars accumulated during his decades-long service as a commander with Iran's elite special forces, reached out in early 2026, deliberations ensued: Could he have been sent to feed DW misinformation and lies to discredit the broadcaster, whose Farsi service is officially sanctioned in Iran? Could he be trying to harm DW or its Iranian employees?

Over the course of months, journalists from DW's investigative unit and Persian department corresponded with him. Omid shared records and photos of his training, which ranged from sniper practice and surveillance to street fighting, riot control and parachuting courses. He also provided photos and videos, documents and locations of a secret monitoring center and housing compounds reserved for high-ranking members of the Iranian security forces.
United in their absolute loyalty to Iran's supreme leader, he said, a clandestine circle of high-ranking officers plot and execute the murder and abductions of the regime's opponents.

Omid's testimony offered a rare insight into Iran's powerful and opaque security apparatus — and into the lives of the men at the core of the Islamic Republic — allowing DW to piece together a picture of how the regime has maintained deeply loyal forces despite widespread protest movements, international sanctions, rising inflation and recent attacks by its two main enemies, Israel and the United States, that eliminated much of its top military and political leadership.

DW corroborated substantial parts of Omid's account with documents, photos, videos and interviews with experts. An intermediary connected the investigative team with a second high-ranking defector, whose account corroborated key details provided by Omid. Though DW confirmed both men's identities, we are withholding certain details to protect them and their families.

blocks.caption: "Omid" and "Reza" provided images and documentsImage: Privat

blocks.text: In the past, Iran has gone after dissidents and opposition activists abroad, including journalists.
We asked the Embassy or Iran in Berlin and the Supreme Leader’s Office to respond to our findings. The Supreme Leader's Office did not reply.
The embassy in Berlin declined to address the individual allegations, stating that "the Islamic Republic of Iran firmly rejects these allegations and the conclusions drawn from them."
Prayers and privileges

As a high-ranking member of the special forces, Omid had access to the privileges the regime often bestows upon its own: From financial incentives and lucrative economic contracts for their own enterprises to special housing compounds, with their own mosques, schools and hospitals, where personal satellite dishes are banned and religious observance is enforced.

blocks.caption: Omid's training included parachuting courses. Image: Privat

blocks.text: These privileges have their price, Omid said: "control, nothing but control." Officers are tightly monitored. "You're not allowed to just attend a wedding or travel," he said. "They confiscate your passport; they even decide which schools your children are allowed to attend."

The control extends to soldiers' prospective partners, who are first vetted by the regime. Even then, Omid said, he was not allowed to share the true nature of his work with his wife. That, he said, "really eats away at you."

By separating such agents from regular Iranians, the regime can keep a closer eye on its forces, said Saeid Golkar, political scientist at the University of Tennessee, who has extensively researched the command structure of the Islamic Republic's security apparatus. "They can create peer pressure and indoctrinate much more effectively," Golkar told DW.
And, Golkar said, security forces who are largely segregated from regular Iranians are less likely to balk at using force against their civilian compatriots.
A defector from Iran's intelligence agency

A month into DW's interactions with Omid, an intermediary connected us with another high-ranking defector. The man, whom we're calling Reza, worked with the Information Ministry, Iran's intelligence agency.

Like many who are recruited into the security apparatus, Reza hails from a religious family: He grinned as he showed DW a picture on his phone of himself as a young man, sporting the long beard and turban favored by the devout in Iran.

blocks.caption: "Reza" used to be an ardent supporter of the Iranian regime. Image: DW

blocks.text: Many of his relatives, he said, still occupy prominent positions in the Iranian regime.

In the early days, he was an ardent supporter of the regime and would sometimes cry during prayers, he said, knowing that he was serving his people and the Islamic Republic and "might even die as a martyr for Islam."

Reza said he slowly turned against the regime as he witnessed the clampdown on protesters. Over the years, officers have shot, arrested and beaten Iranians protesting the country's deteriorating living conditions and strict "morality" laws.
Nowadays, his hair is cropped short.
'Years serving a cruel system'

On the evening of January 8, amid an almost total internet shutdown, security forces opened fire on Iranians protesting widespread shortages and spiking inflation. The extent of the massacre slowly came to light as images trickled out of the country documenting the regime's atrocities.

blocks.caption: In January 2026, protesters took to the streets again. Image: UGC/DW

blocks.text: Thousands of protesters were killed across Iran. Both Omid and Reza said the mass killings which, human rights organizations report, included the shooting of unarmed protesters in hospital beds — had horrified them.
Indeed, this ongoing brutality ultimately led them to speak with DW.
Omid was adamant that he had never shot at protesters nor ordered his subordinates to do so, although DW is unable to corroborate this.
When pressed, he conceded that he had witnessed the killing of demonstrators.

Reza said the guilt he carried after having "wasted 10, 11 years serving a cruel system" compelled him to speak out despite the risk to him and his family. "The truth is: When your opponent is a regime that doesn't adhere to any moral values, you need to be prepared for anything," he said.
Who are Iran's Revolutionary Guards?
Surveillance and suppression

Omid and Reza discussed secret command centers that are central to clamping down on protests. High-ranking members of all units and agencies gather in a monitoring room where, Omid and Reza say, huge monitors on the walls display real-time feeds from countless CCTV cameras around the capital, Tehran. They say there are other such rooms around the country.

Protest marches are also monitored from above by drones. And, Reza said, "information from forces on the ground and from Twitter, Telegram and other social networks, as well as information obtained through surveillance and interception devices — all this information is collected there."
Plainclothes agents often infiltrate protest groups. Omid said such agents were sometimes used to redirect protest marches to places where security forces lie in wait.
A representative of Iran's supreme leader "had a free hand" in ordering operations from within the command center, Omid said, as well as deciding "how harshly the protesters should be dealt with."

When regular police can no longer quell demonstrations, Omid and Reza said, elite units from the Revolutionary Guard and police, often clad entirely in black, their faces hidden behind balaclavas, are sent in to finish the job.

blocks.caption: Documents DW obtained reveal the design of forces deployed to quell protestsImage: DW

blocks.text: Human rights organizations have documented the use of automatic and semiautomatic machine guns and even heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks to clamp down on protests.

"The fact that the security forces are equipped with military-grade firearms that were designed for combat situations, for responding to protests, shows that the killings of protesters in the country are intended," finds Amnesty International Iran researcher Raha Bahreini, the author of a recent report analyzing the regime's chain of command during the 2022 protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Aminiin custody.
The Dakhme 'killing machine'

After months of correspondence, Omid pointed DW to an outwardly unremarkable location in Shahr-e Rey, on the outskirts of Tehran: A prayer hall sandwiched between an occupational therapy practice and a pharmacy. Though the prayer hall is named Beit al Shohada, or the house of martyrs, Omid said many officers call the place Dakhme, meaning crypt or tomb.

blocks.caption: The men allegedly meet in this prayer hall on Pilgush StreetImage: Privat

blocks.text: Omid described how high-ranking officers met under Dakhme's corrugated iron roof to plot off-the-books operations that bypass government structures. He said he had attended several meetings at Dakhme "where decisions about murder are made: It's a killing machine."

Though Omid insisted repeatedly that he had only attended the meetings because he had been ordered to by his higher-ups and he had never taken part in any of the operations plotted at Dakhme, he listed murders and abductions within and outside of Iran that he said were planned there. DW could not verify these cases but found that some of the people named had indeed died under unresolved circumstances.

Several experts DW contacted knew of Dakhme in connection with a murder attempt on an adviser to a reformist president over two decades ago. Others had never heard of Dakhme. No one DW spoke with could confirm its continued operation.

Experts agree that a facility such as Dakhme is plausible. "The Islamic Republic probably feels more of a need now to have these types of groups," Miad Maleki, a former US Treasury official who until recently designed US sanctions programs targeting Iran, told DW.
Indeed, Maleki said, military operations planned covertly at Dakhme would likely give the regime plausible deniability in cases of killings.

blocks.caption: DW obtained rare images of a religious gathering inside Dakhme.

blocks.text: Religious and ruthless

Because of the secrecy surrounding Dakhme, much of the following is based only on Omid's accounts and the rare images DW obtained of religious ceremonies inside the hall. The secret meetings usually kick off under the guise of religious ceremonies and rituals, he said, in a large hall often adorned with green drapes and religious banners. After a communal dinner, only those in the inner circle stay.

Those who remain hand over their mobile phones, which are locked away. Then, Omid said, "seasoned specialists from Iran's special forces and intelligence operation " discuss murder and abductions late into the night.

"For these people, a person's position isn't that important," Omid said. "If they consider someone a threat to the supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, they take it extremely seriously and take action."
After each operation, Omid said, the men return to their respective roles within Iran's security apparatus, until they gather again to defend the Islamic Republic at any cost.

articles.title: Marcos touts business, energy investments after Singapore visit
articles.summary: Marcos highlights investment deals with Singapore-based firms.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:58pm
This screenshot photo shows President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivering an arrival statement upon his return to the Philippines on October 12, 2026 after a five-day working visit in Singapore.
RTVM / Philstar.com's screenshot
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. highlighted the investment commitments from Singapore-based firms upon his arrival in the Philippines after a five-day working visit.
Marcos arrived back in the country at around 1:54 a.m. on Monday, October 12, The STAR reported.

In his arrival statement, Marcos said he met with executives of FedEx, Mitsubishi Corp. and Vena Energy during his visit to Singapore, where investment pledges for the Philippine business and energy sectors were discussed.
Business investments

According to Marcos, Mitsubishi’s $700 million investment in Ayala Corp. was a significant deal, as it is “expected to be among the largest foreign equity investments in the Philippines in recent years.”
The recent deal would reportedly increase Mitsubishi’s ownership stake in Ayala Corp. from 4.7% to 15%.
Meanwhile, Marcos said FedEx had expressed strong interest in expanding its Clark Gateway Hub in Pampanga, which is expected to open in the last quarter of 2028.

This expansion, the president added, is set to help small and medium enterprises, or MSMEs, sell their products in the international market through the facility’s increased capacity to handle more air cargo and specialized shipments.
Renewable energy expansion
For the energy sector, Vena Energy had expressed its intention to expand its presence in the Philippines, which Marcos said is in line with the country’s energy agenda.

The president said the firm is planning to build more facilities that generate electricity from renewable sources to add generating capacity to its existing operations and produce up to 1.29 gigawatts of power.
Vena Energy is planning to invest P52 billion in this expansion project over the next two years, Marcos added.
The company’s existing operations in the Philippines include operational facilities with a combined capacity of 887 megawatts and other projects under construction with a capacity of 1.26 gigawatts.
Marcos said the investment pledge is aligned with the government’s goal of achieving a 35% renewable energy share in the country’s power supply by 2030 and 50% by 2040.

“I am confident that the interest shown by investors in these engagements will bring more high value investments, partnerships, technology, and jobs to the Philippines, particularly in sectors that will support our long-term growth and transformation,” Marcos said.
Nuclear energy plans. Meanwhile, Marcos said he also visited the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute to learn from the country’s studies on nuclear energy as a power source.
Marcos has consistently expressed support for integrating nuclear energy into the country’s power mix to lower electricity costs.
His push for nuclear energy has drawn criticism and concerns, especially from environmental advocates, over safety, radioactive waste management and financial risks.

articles.title: Melbourne Islamic leader silent on centre’s alleged Flydubai hijacker links in Facebook video
articles.summary:
MyCentre leader Samir Mohtadi, who also goes by Abu Hamza, refers to Islamic texts on the virtues of staying silent

  • Get our

blocks.text: A leader of a Melbourne Islamic centre allegedly linked to the accused Flydubai hijacker has released a video extolling the virtues of staying silent, without directly commenting on the accusations from prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, the attorney general of the UAE, on the weekend said that investigators had traced the ideological and professional background of the 29-year-old suspect and that their findings indicated his “drift towards extremism and terrorism” began while he was studying at RMIT University in Melbourne in 2017.

He alleged the co-pilot, Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, had said that while studying in Melbourne he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with RMIT, and through those visits had become acquainted with people associated with a centre known as “MyCentre”. He allegedly said that the centre was managed by a man known as “Abu Hamza” but the UAE attorney general did not state whether the suspect had ever met Abu Hamza.
There was no allegation that anyone at the centre was involved in radicalising al-Hammami or had kept in contact with him or had any knowledge of his intentions before the 30 September flight.
On Sunday night, MyCentre’s leader, Samir Mohtadi – who also goes by Abu Hamza – appeared in a four-minute video released on the centre’s Facebook page.

He refers to Islamic texts on the virtues of staying silent when being attacked by others but makes no reference to the alleged Flydubai hijack attempt, the UAE attorney general’s statement or to al-Hammami.
“You’ll find those who are righteous you’ll always find have been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned, and this is the way it is,” Mohtadi says in the video.

He referred to the stories of Mariam, known to Christians as Mary, the mother of Jesus, being subject to criticism and attack but saying “I’m not going to speak to anyone” and “I’m going to fast from talking”.

“There are circumstances, my beloved brothers and respected sisters, regardless how much you explain yourself to people, that’s it, they’re fixated with their ideas and that’s it, you can’t change them,” Mohtadi said.
“So the best thing, sometimes, is not to say anything.”
Mohtadi has been contacted for comment.

RMIT has confirmed al-Hammami had studied engineering at the university, but left Australia before completing the qualification. He subsequently underwent flight training in New Zealand and became a qualified commercial pilot.
after newsletter promotion

Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop the alleged attempt to hijack the plane and crash it into Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv in a “premeditated terrorist plot”, according to the UAE attorney general’s statement.
According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001.
“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said.

Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.

Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country, with New Zealand authorities also examining his time there between November 2018 and May 2019.

On Sunday, Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the co-pilot was allegedly radicalised online. He also said the government wanted to properly screen people at the border and in online settings.

articles.title: [EDITORIAL] Ang tunay na collateral damage sa umano’y undisclosed wealth ni Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Napakalaki ng P817 million in undeclared assets — it boggles the mind — hindi na ito clerical oversight

blocks.text: Napakalaki ng P817 million in undeclared assets — it boggles the mind — hindi na ito clerical oversight
“Collateral damage.” ‘Yan ang Vietnam war term ng US military na tumutukoy sa mga hindi sinasadyang namatay, nasugatan, o naperwisyo sa isang military action.

blocks.caption: AnimatEd, editorial,Sara Duterte, Mans Carpio, Hidden wealth, undisclosed wealth, corruption, impeachment

blocks.text: Sabi ni Mans Carpio, ang asawa ni Vice President Sara Duterte, collateral damage daw siya. Mr. Carpio, akala mo ba’y sibilyan kang nadaplisan ng bala sa labanang hindi mo nilikha?

Hindi ka sibilyan o bystander. Central actor ka sa gulo. Malinaw ang absolute community property principle sa batas — conjugal property ang lahat ng ari-arian ninyong mag-asawa kung walang pre-nuptial agreement, at dapat idineklara sa Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) ng iyong asawa.

Kung sinusundan ninyo ang impeachment trial, napakaraming insurance policies — 19 to be exact — ang kinuha ni Carpio para sa kanyang asawa. Is he monetizing his wife’s risk appetite o mayroon siyang alam na hindi alam ng lahat? Whatever. Sa 19 insurance policies, 17 ang hindi idineklara ni Sara Duterte sa kanyang SALN.

Anong klaseng esposo ang biglang nagpapaawa at dumidistansiya sa kanyang kabiyak ngayong sinisilip ang kanilang finances? Laglagan time na ba talaga? Kung sabagay, inilaglag din ng defense team ni Sara si Carpio at ang amang si Rodrigo Duterte. Sabi ng defense team, hindi raw alam ni Sara na kumuha ng sandamakmak na insurance policies ang kabiyak. Sa kaso naman ng joint account shared with Digong, wala raw alam ang Bise Presidente na may ganoong accounts sa Bank of the Philippine Islands, Julia Vargas branch sa Pasig.

Ang ipinagtataka namin, bakit hindi man lang nag-effort si Sara Duterte sa pagpi-fill out ng kanyang SALN over the years? Abogado naman siya, alam na alam niya ang kahalagahan ng SALN filing sa isang public official. Si dating chief justice Maria Lourdes “Meilou” Sereno nga, nasipa sa pagiging CJ at nabura ang rekord na siya’y minsang naging CJ, dahil sa hindi pagpa-file ng SALNs nang siya’y professor sa University of the Philippines.

Hindi ba sineryoso ang pagfa-file ng SALN o talagang hindi kayang maikukubli ang P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025? Oo nga naman, how do you pass off or rationalize P817 million in wealth without legitimate income sources?

Halimbawa, paanong nag-generate ang isang kompanyang tulad ng banana chips company na Cale88 Foods Corp. ng P208 million in sales mula 2021-2025? Samantala zero employees ito noong 2023 at 2024, at dalawa lang ang empleyado pagdating ng 2025?
Public office is a public trust. Kailangang tumalima ang mga nasa poder sa pinakamataas na pamantayan ng transparency and accountability.

Napakalaki ng P817 million in undeclared assets — it boggles the mind — hindi na ito clerical oversight. For comparison ng halaga, itinuturing ng batas na plunder o pandarambong at hindi na simpleng graft ang pangungulimbat ng minimum P50 million. Bakit mo itatago ang P817 million kung hindi naman ito galing sa masama?

Again, teka lang, ayon naman kay dating senador Sonny Trillanes at Senador Risa Hontiveros, nasa P319 milyon umano ang dumaloy sa Cale88 mula sa Chinese government at China-based corporations. Foreign power ba ang source ng bahagi ng unexplained wealth?
Pero balik tayo sa P817 million in undeclared assets. Nagpapakita ito ng arrogance of power. Masisilip mo rito ang hubris na nag-overestimate ng kapangyarihan niya at bumale-wala sa warning signs.
Wala bang pakialam sa batas si Sara Duterte dahil buong buhay niya’y prinsesa siya ng Davao at walang nangahas na kantiin ang anak ni Rodrigo Duterte? Ngayon pa ba na bise presidente siya?
Warak na warak na ang naratibong “simpleng tao” si Sara Duterte. Sa likod ng populist persona, lumilitaw ang Sara na umano’y hayok na hayok pala sa pera.
Kapag nag-o-operate ang public servants sa assumption na immune sila sa public scrutiny, lalo pang nababakbak ang tiwala ng taumbayan.
At ang tunay na “collateral damage” ay ang 32.2 milyong Pilipinong bumoto kay Sara noong 2022.
Ang may psychological bullet in the head ngayon ay ang 61.53% ng voters noong 2022 na naniwalang simpleng tao si Sara Duterte. #Panagutin. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte leads 2028 presidential preferences in Pulse Asia survey
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte emerged as the most preferred presidential candidate for the May 2028 national elections, with half of Filipino adults choosing her in a September 2026 Pulse Asia survey.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 12:22pm
Vice President Sara Duterte emerged as the most preferred presidential candidate for the May 2028 national elections, with half of Filipino adults choosing her in a September 2026 Pulse Asia survey.
The survey, conducted from September 17 to 24, showed Duterte leading seven potential presidential contenders with 50% voter preference.
Duterte registered her strongest support in Mindanao at 92%, followed by the Visayas at 56%, the National Capital Region (NCR) at 40%, and the rest of Luzon at 28%.
Former Vice President Leni Robredo ranked second with 26%, followed by Senator Raffy Tulfo at 12% and Senator Risa Hontiveros at 3%.
Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon each received 1%, while Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong garnered 0.3%.
Three percent of respondents were undecided, another 3% said they would not support any of the potential candidates, while 1% declined to express a preference.
'Alternative scenarios'
Duterte also maintained her lead in all five alternative scenarios presented to respondents for the 2028 presidential race.
In a three-way contest involving Duterte, Robredo, and Tulfo, the Vice President received 52% voter preference, compared with Robredo's 30% and Tulfo's 14%.
Duterte recorded particularly strong support in Mindanao at 94%, followed by the Visayas at 55%.
By socioeconomic class, she received 50% support among Class D (lower-income) respondents and 70% among Class E (the poorest socioeconomic group) respondents.
The survey also showed Duterte leading in four other hypothetical presidential contests:

items: Duterte (57%), Tulfo (17%), and Hontiveros (14%)
Duterte (57%), Tulfo (18%), and Senator Bam Aquino (16%)
Duterte (54%) and Robredo (40%)
Duterte (60%) and Hontiveros (23%)

blocks.text: Impeachment proceedings
The survey was conducted as the Senate impeachment court heard evidence on Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth and business interests under Article II of the impeachment complaint.
During the survey period, prosecutors presented corporate and government procurement records involving companies linked to the Vice President.
On September 23, the impeachment court also ruled that senators physically unable to attend the hearings would be excluded in determining the number of votes required to convict Duterte.

Article II of the impeachment complaint accused the Vice President of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over allegations that she amassed unexplained wealth, failed to truthfully disclose her assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), and failed to divest herself of business interests as required under the Constitution.
Pulse Asia reportedly interviewed 2,400 Filipino adults nationwide through face-to-face interviews.

The survey had a ±2-percentage-point margin of error at the 95% confidence level. Subnational estimates for Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao each had a ±4-percentage-point margin of error, the survey firm said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Remulla to Supreme Court: Time to review anti-plunder law amid flood control scandal
articles.summary: In his first year at the Office of the Ombudsman, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has urged the Supreme Court to revisit the anti-plunder law.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 12:19pm

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla speaks to reporters after taking his oath before Supreme Court Associate Justice Marvic Leonen as the new Ombudsman during a ceremony at the Supreme Court in Manila on Wednesday, Oct. 9, 2025.
The STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — In his first year at the Office of the Ombudsman, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has urged the Supreme Court to revisit the anti-plunder law.
In his speech on Monday, October 12, Remulla said that securing convictions faces a major legal hurdle: the 2016 Supreme Court ruling in Macapagal-Arroyo v. People.
“Kaya sinasabi ko ito nang may buong paggalang sa Kataas-taasang Hukuman: panahon na para balikan ang doktrinang ito. It is time to revisit it,” Remulla said in his speech.
(That is why I say this with all due respect to the Supreme Court: it is time to revisit this doctrine. It is time to revisit it.)

The doctrine, according to Remulla, introduced two requirements not originally written by Congress into the plunder law: first, that the prosecution must identify a "main plunderer"; and second, that it must prove the accused personally received or benefited from the stolen funds.
“Think about what that means. The smarter the thief, the safer he is. Pass the money through enough dummies, middlemen and shell companies, and no one can be shown to have touched it,” Remulla said.
He argued that while the plunder law was designed to hold those who steal billions accountable, the current doctrine makes the largest syndicates the hardest to catch.
“Hindi po iyan hustisya. Pananggalang po iyan,” he said.
(That is not justice. That is a shield.)
Remulla added that the ongoing flood control cases mirror the complex, multi-layered schemes protected by the current plunder doctrine.
“Let us not forget the size and magnitude of this scandal. Over a hundred billion pesos was paid for flood control projects that were never built,” Remulla said.
“Hindi substandard. Hindi kulang. Wala talaga,” he added.
(Not substandard. Not lacking. There is nothing at all.)
Philstar.com has reached out to the Supreme Court for comment on Remulla’s pronouncement, but it has yet to reply.

articles.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK spending pressures
articles.summary:
Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year

John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that…

blocks.text: John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.

As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.

Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.
Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”

Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt, the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.

Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.
“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.

Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”
Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.

“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”
Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.

With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.

Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.

The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.
after newsletter promotion
However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.

Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.

The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.
“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”
She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.
“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

articles.title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded promo ads of Trump
articles.summary: Last week, President Donald Trump said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great USA."

image.caption: Trump said he considered the ads to be 'rather standard'Image: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television ads paid for with millions in taxpayer money for political promotions, a federal court judge ruled on Sunday night, granting a temporary restraining order.
This comes after publicly funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking bipartisan backlash.
The commercials feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."
They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.
What did the judge say?
New York District Judge Jennifer L Rochon called the commercials an illegal misuse of funds, siding with a coalition which includes the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.

The court ordered the halt even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end. In a court filing late on Saturday, the Justice Department had argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."
What is the controversy?
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million (€17.8 million) taxpayer funds to run the ads in question.
Legal experts argue that it violates a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda," along with other laws potentially.
On Monday, Trump had said he considered the ads to be "rather standard" and a "positive promotion for our great USA," but that they would not be funded by taxpayers any longer.
The White House said last week that the president's political action committee would fund the ads going forward but not reimburse taxpayers for the ones that had already run on their dime.
Trump proclaims US 'golden age' of science

"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit organization that represents them.

"We won't stop until this administration is ‌held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste ‌and ​abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomon.

The plaintiffs, which included a public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, urged the judge to block the ads by Friday so they would not air during weekend programming, such as football games and Saturday Night Live.
US Democrats have also challeneged the ads in a seperate suit filed at a federal court in Washington.

articles.title: Marcos back in PH following working visit in Singapore
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. returned to the Philippines on Monday after his working visit to Singapore, where he discussed cargo and energy expansion and investment opportunities with…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 11:47am

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. returned to the Philippines on Monday after his working visit to Singapore, where he discussed cargo and energy expansion and investment opportunities with business leaders.
In his arrival statement, Marcos said he met business leaders, including officials from FedEx, Mitsubishi Corporation, and Vena Energy.
During his meeting with FedEx, Marcos said the company plans to expand its Clark Gateway Hub in Pampanga, which is scheduled to open in the fourth quarter of 2028.
“The expanded hub will significantly increase capacity for international air freight and specialized cargo, helping our micro, small and medium enterprises reach global markets,” Marcos said.
He also announced that Mitsubishi Corporation will invest $700 million in Ayala Corporation, which is “expected to be among the largest foreign equity investments in the Philippines in recent years.”
Meanwhile, Vena Energy plans to add 1.29 gigawatts of capacity, backed by a P52-billion equity investment over the next two years.
“This is on top of an existing 887 megawatt operational capacity and about 1.26 gigawatts under construction,” the President said.
“These developments directly align with our goal of achieving a 35% renewable energy share in power generation by 2030 and 50% by the year 2040,” he added.
Marcos earlier said his working visit to Singapore from October 7 to 11 would help prepare the Philippines for the industries of the future.
He also participated in the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference, where he engaged with government and business leaders from other countries, including Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Presenting the Philippines’ economic priorities, Marcos said he shared the country’s growing exports, efforts to ease doing business, and plans to strengthen its technological capabilities through research and development.

He added that he highlighted the country’s resolve to fight corruption, strengthen digital safeguards, build strong international economic ties, protect its sovereignty, sovereign rights, and jurisdiction in the West Philippine Sea, and contribute to regional peace and stability.

“Our objective is not simply to attract investments today. We must also prepare the energy supply, the infrastructure, technology, and human capital necessary to sustain the industries of tomorrow,” Marcos said.
“To power our growth, we will keep studying all viable options for our long-term energy security and build the technical capability to make informed decisions for our future,” he added.
The President also visited the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute, where he said he learned about Singapore’s work in nuclear research, technology, and safety.

“We returned home having strengthened an important partnership, opened new opportunities for investment and cooperation, and advanced our preparations for the economy that we want to build for the Filipino people,” Marcos said. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Comelec assumes chairmanship of international orgs
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday announced that the Philippines will assume the chairmanship of the Association of World Election Bodies (A-WEB) and the Association of Asian Election…

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 11:39am

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday announced that the Philippines will assume the chairmanship of the Association of World Election Bodies (A-WEB) and the Association of Asian Election Authorities (AAEA).

“In a historic first, the Philippines will simultaneously take on the leadership of both organizations, placing Comelec at the forefront of global and regional cooperation in electoral administration,” it said in a statement.
According to Comelec, A-WEB is a global association of election management bodies while AAEA brings together election authorities across Asia.

It said that the chairmanship is expected to provide new opportunities for Comelec to strengthen its partnerships with its international counterparts and facilitate the exchange of electoral expertise.
Comelec said the turnover will take place during gatherings hosted by Comelec from October 12 to 18 in Makati City.

“As the incoming Chair of both organizations, the Comelec through the stewardship of Chairman Garcia will lead efforts to advance cooperation among the member bodies, particularly involving electoral integrity, technological innovation, cybersecurity, and misinformation and disinformation, among others.
According to Comelec, the A-WEB x AAEA International Conference and the A-WEB General Assembly will simultaneously take place on October 15 while the AAEA General Assembly will be on October 17.

“This International Conference will serve as a platform for member election management bodies of both international organizations to engage in a meaningful discussion, exchange knowledge and best practices, and share perspectives on contemporary issues in electoral administration,” it said.
Comelec said it will also present the “Manila Declaration.”
“The declaration is intended for the formal adoption and ceremonial signing by authorized representatives of the participating election management bodies,” it said. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Pulse Asia: 89% of Pinoys interested in May 2028 elections
articles.summary: Nearly nine out of 10, or 89% of Filipinos are interested in the May 2028 national and local elections, the latest survey from Pulse Asia showed.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 11:31am
Nearly nine out of 10, or 89% of Filipinos are interested in the May 2028 national and local elections, the latest survey from Pulse Asia showed.

Of this figure, 57% are truly interested, while 31% are somewhat interested in the said elections, according to the results of the Ulat ng Bayan national survey on the May 2028 elections conducted by Pulse Asia from September 17 to 24, 2026.
Seven percent meanwhile cannot say whether they are interested or not, while 4% are disinterested — 3% somewhat disinterested, and 1% truly disinterested, the survey showed.
The 2028 national and local elections will be held on May 8, less than two years away from the time the survey was conducted.
The Commission on Elections said earlier this year that the 2028 elections will push through.
Geographical areas
In the National Capital Region (NCR), 87% are interested in the May 2028 elections, comprised of 57% truly interested and 31% somewhat interested.
The figures are almost the same in Balance Luzon (the rest of Luzon excluding NCR) and Visayas. In Balance Luzon, 85% of respondents are interested, while 89% are interested in Visayas.
In Mindanao, however, 97% of respondents said they are interested in the May 2028 elections, with 82% truly interested and 15% somewhat interested.
Classes
Across income classes, interest in the May 2028 elections is high.
It is 88% among the ABC classes, of which 59% are truly interested, and 28% somewhat interested.
Among the Class D, 89% of respondents said they are truly interested (56% truly interested, and 34% somewhat interested).
Class E respondents on the other hand had 87% interested (69% truly interested, and 18% somewhat interested).
Survey details
Pulse Asia conducted the survey using face-to-face interviews among 2,400 respondents aged 18 years old and above.
The survey had a margin of error of ± 2% at the 95% confidence level.
Meanwhile, for geographical areas, subnational estimates of the margin of error at the 95% confidence level are: ± 4% for Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. —KG, GMA News

items: At least 139 migrants, including 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat capsized while traveling from Djibouti to Yemen, with 82 survivors reported.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) highlighted the dangers faced by migrants in the region, as many continue to undertake perilous journeys despite ongoing violence in Yemen and Ethiopia.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

NAIROBI, Kenya – At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration said on Sunday, October 11.
The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock, a port town in Djibouti, during the night of October 8-9, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts.

Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. A spokesperson for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore.
“Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” said IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac.
“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities,” Coissac said.

Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased.
The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment.

The migrants were heading to Yemen, hoping eventually to reach wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals flee their own country, which is experiencing its most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
“Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries,” the IOM statement said.
Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month, marking the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years.
“People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time,” the official said.

Ethiopian migrants interviewed for the agency’s most recent situation report on Djibouti, covering September 20 to September 30, said they had left their country because of difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought.
“Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces,” the report said.
Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on September 23, have told Reuters they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruiting young men into the defense forces.
The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment.

The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war, with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia’s government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance.

The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to the IOM’s Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18%.

The IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week.
More than 3,700 people had fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said. – Rappler.com
