An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday, October 9, detailing Claude models’ unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites.

It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms.
The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate network hacks by AI agents, and researchers’ warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity.

Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties were.

“Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X.
This process was “not optional,” he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility.

The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called “unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems”.
On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions to an automated testing process.
“The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable,” they said.
The July 18 tip purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, police added.
“I may have information regarding this case,” Anthropic’s model wrote in its submission.

“I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” The brackets featured in Anthropic’s statement.
Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another.
In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university.
Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs.
Philadelphia police said the tip “was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination.”
Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies “a person”, however.
This includes “information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident.”
Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide.
Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems or compromise of their data. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Newspoint] A running commentary
articles.summary: The defense in Sara Duterte’s trial is succeeding in dragging it out by playing to the vulnerabilities of a court apparently afraid to be seen as less than fair. Understandably, a court composed…

blocks.text: I’ve been doing a running commentary on the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. In the beginning, I set my comments down for my own professional purposes, as an opinion writer for this news site and as a prospective resource interviewee in other forums. But lately, as the proceedings have become more interesting, of urgent popular interest, and less tedious — although, still, less tedious only in parts — I have been posting my comments on certain online threads.

Since I’m published here only once every fortnight, I’m scarcely able to comment on those occurrences in good time. Considering, therefore, their fair removal from the actual occurrences, these views, having been necessarily hurriedly posted in their original, needed to be reset in context or clarified here.

In any case, to set the original from the additions, I have put the latter in brackets, as professional form prescribes. The subtitles, although unbracketed in keeping with house style, are additions themselves.
And so, here goes:

[Davao City Mayor] Baste [Duterte] tries to look confident and knowledgeable, but comes across…as inconsistent and self-contradictory. He says he does not know, but ends up showing it impossible for him to not have known [as in the case of granting city contracts to a corporation one of whose principal owners is a close family and political associate, indeed a corporation of which his sister Sara is herself, by her own admission, part owner].

All Baste needed to memorize for his testimony was that he knew nothing and variations [of expressing that professed ignorance], which should have required not much memory work and no mental work altogether. [Still, in one blank moment, he needs to be rescued by the court president, Chiz Escudero, who prompts him: Would he have granted a corporation any contracts if he had known that his sister had anything to do with it?]

When Chiz said “the senators” preferred [the former senator Antonio] Trillanes did not testify, which senators was he referring to? [This utterance I had learned from sources privy to the relevant conversations.]

I cannot quite understand how it is proper at all for the court to say it wishes anyone not testifying, especially someone like Trillanes, whose exposé alleging various crimes committed by the Dutertes has been validated…. If the senators Chiz referred to included majority senators, and with the prosecution panel going along, the suspicion cannot be helped that all of them were played. And Chiz being a turncoat [from the minority, along with Joel Villanueva] and now himself the impeachment court president, who could have been playing whom?

Possibly, just possibly, keeping Trillanes out avoids [as apologists say] his being shown as having turned up findings from his own investigations, therefore unofficial and only likely to be shot down as inadmissible by Chiz, who as court president tends to apply those standards more strictly than intended for an impeachment court.

Whatever the possibilities, and given how Chiz went so easy on Baste as to help him look innocent about his sister’s connection to the company he had awarded contracts to, Chiz cannot help attracting suspicions about his leanings.
I guess the ultimate test comes when the final vote is taken — guilty or not?

[About defense lawyer Mark Vinluan’s warning that, under the law on confidential information, the press could get into trouble if it made public certain information from bank records:] Since, according to the Constitution, “no law shall be passed abridging the freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press,” I hold that it is a matter of public duty for the press to make public any information in the public interest, regardless of any law stopping the press fulfilling that duty, for in that case such a law constitutes the precise sort of abridgment disallowed by the Constitution.

The defense in Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial is succeeding in dragging it out by playing to the vulnerabilities of a court apparently afraid to be seen as less than fair. Understandably, a court composed mostly of members of the political majority is not unlikely to feel that way.

But the reality…is that an impeachment trial is as much a judicial as a political trial, in fact, more political than judicial in practical terms. After all, it is intended as an exigent process, undertaken not to prove any crime but only to judge the fitness of a high official to remain in office. For, unstopped, that official, if guilty as impeached and until so judged, poses a continuing grave…danger not only to her office but to the nation.
Subsequently, anyway, criminal accountability is to be proven in a regular court.

Finally, China, the communist world power to which President Duterte ceded control of the strategic and mineral-rich West Philippine Sea, has begun to emerge as an issue in the impeachment trial. It had been buried in the trial and even in the off-court discourse inspired by it until Trillanes, who had been trying to call proportionate attention to it, found an outside forum to discuss it. He pointed to Chinese money funneled through bank accounts traced to the Dutertes — the transactions had in fact been flagged — and donated to a foundation on whose board Sara Duterte herself sits.

At the trial, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros pursued the issue, but it has yet to gain the traction it deserves. Understandably, It continues to be overshadowed by issues more directly relevant to the impeachment.

But the China-Duterte connection poses to the nation dangers no less grave or urgent than does a guilty Sara Duterte continuing in office. In fact, China and the Dutertes are mutually reinforcing inimical forces. Nothing, therefore, should stop watchdog institutions, the press in particular, taking up China as a separate horror story.

If any revelation stands out [in Wednesday’s hearing], it is the unfamiliar banking practice that allows clients to conceal the true sizes of their accounts. It ought to be a particular help to public officials who naturally wish to be seen poorer than they actually are in at least the one document they are required to submit for public scrutiny — the Statement of Assets and Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN)

The trick consists in a client buying a manager’s check, whose amount is taken out automatically from the client’s account. Meantime, the check remains parked in a sort of limbo account, unencashed, waiting to be redeemed by the client once the purpose for the concealment has been achieved — in the case of a public official, [an obviously] willful but normally untraceable net-worth misdeclaration.

For a more knowledgeable and insightful observation, a retired banker friend adds: “Manager’s checks are equivalent to cash, obviat[ing] the necessity to clear ordinary check payments and wait for…two-day clearance…it is a necessary and convenient tool in making payments of large amounts…a facilitator of commercial transactions, which the criminal mind has perverted and used for its own crooked ends. Perhaps the manner of SALN reporting needs to change…. Police work is not [in] banking’s nature.”

The defense is making life unnecessarily difficult for us home viewers. It wants especially those of us who take a particular interest in the proceedings [to bother] to take down notes ourselves, instead of allowing us to simply to photograph the exhibits flashed on the screen. If those exhibits are allowed to be presented in whatever other form, shouldn’t they be allowed to be flashed on the screen as the prosecution wishes — for at least the sakes of old and slow viewers like me?

[One online thread participant remarks: “Not just for the sake of ‘old and slow viewers’ like us but also for many who are not used to long, laborious expositions nor have the patience for them.” To which, I replied:] Well, I’m one specific objector. Others can choose to object on their own or just sit back and allow Chiz Escudero to take them for fools. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Robert Pether was detained in Iraq in 2021 and his family feared he would die in jail. Now he’s coming home
articles.summary: Australian foreign minister welcomes Iraqi government’s decision to allow engineer to leave Baghdad

blocks.text: Australian engineer Robert Pether has been allowed to leave Iraq after a four-year stint in a Baghdad jail cell that his family feared would kill him.

Pether’s family say they have been “living in hell” since he was arrested without charge in April 2021 in connection to a business dispute between his firm – which was building a new headquarters for the central bank – and the Iraqi government.
He was imprisoned for more than four years but then released mid-last year due to his deteriorating health. He was banned from leaving the country.
The Australian foreign minister, Penny Wong, confirmed on Monday that Pether had now been allowed to leave the country. It was understood he was in transit.
“The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government’s decision to allow Mr Robert Pether to leave Iraq today,” Wong said.
“I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family.”
“Today’s outcome follows many years of persistent advocacy by the Australian government, including at the highest levels of government, and sustained consular assistance to Mr Pether and his family.”

Pether and his colleague Khalid Radwan were detained in Baghdad in April 2021 after flying in for a meeting with bank officials to resolve a dispute they were having with his engineering firm, CME Consulting.
Pether was later sentenced and fined over allegations that his firm spent money that should have gone to an architect and a subcontractor.
In a report in March 2022, the United Nations working group on arbitrary detention found Pether had been arbitrarily detained in breach of international law.

The UN body also found the arrest constituted an “enforced disappearance” and may have involved forms of torture. The working group said it had received complaints that Pether “was exposed to extreme cold, threats of death, humiliation and various forms of psychological abuse.”

“Mr Pether was detained in a [2x2 metre] cell with the lights permanently on,” the working group said in its report. “He was reportedly blindfolded, interrogated, screamed at, threatened, insulted and shown torture rooms.”
Pether’s family described the arrest and ongoing detention as a living nightmare.

It caused dramatic deterioration to Pether’s health. In 2022, the Guardian obtained an emotional letter from Pether to his family, penned from behind bars. The letter warned his family that his prognosis was “bleak” and that he was facing a potential “death sentence”.
after newsletter promotion
Pether also wrote of his daily torment about how he should break it to his children that he might not be coming home.

“How do you tell a little girl who loves unicorns and cats that her daddy will not be coming home? How do you tell your children that you are proud of them but will not be sharing the accolades (and pitfalls) of their lives with them?,” Pether wrote.
“And toughest of all, how do you tell your wife, who is very much the other half of you, that you will not be keeping the promise you made to grow old together?”

His wife, Desree, who resides in Ireland, had previously been critical of the efforts of Australian officials to secure his release, but the Australian government said it had raised the case with Iraqi authorities more than 200 times.
Following her husband’s release last year, Desree said she was “grateful to everyone who contributed to this happening”.
The UN working group also posed serious questions about the conduct of Pether’s trial.

The 2022 report aired allegations that Pether’s evidence was mistranslated to indicate guilt and said that even during the trial “Pether and Radwan did not have clarity around their charges”, with charges being dropped during the hearing and replaced with others.

“In the light of the above, the Working Group concludes that the violations of the right to a fair trial and due process are of such gravity as to give the deprivation of liberty of Messrs Pether and Radwan is arbitrary,” the report said.

blocks.text: Gasoline and diesel markets in Asia also face pressure from tighter Chinese supply. China briefly stopped exports of gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel at the start of October as it sought to rebuild domestic inventories, constricting an already strained regional market.
Exports have since resumed, with China approving around 3.7 million metric tons of the three fuels for October, slightly below the 4 million tons or more shipped in September.

China is the world’s largest oil refining market by capacity and an important source of fuel for the Philippines. In 2025, it supplied 3.78 billion liters, or about 20% of the country’s imported finished petroleum products, second only to South Korea.

Local pump prices also remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ERC orders Meralco to refund P2.64 billion to customers
articles.summary: The Energy Regulatory Commission directed Meralco to refund around P2.64 billion in excess charges to its consumers.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 10:37am
Linemen install new transformers on an electric post along United Nations Avenue in Manila on March 22, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has directed the Manila Electric Company (Meralco) on Monday, October 12, to refund around P2.64 billion in excess charges to its consumers.
The refund is expected to reduce bills by an average of P0.1020 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) for at least six months, according to the ERC.
The refund rates, however, differ according to customer class:

items: Flat streetlights - P0.1764 per kWh
Residential and General Service A - P0.1733 per kWh
General Service B - P0.1147 per kWh
Government hospitals, metered streetlights, and charitable institutions - P0.0706 per kWh
General Power - P0.514 per kWh
Generator Wheeling - P0.0128 per kWh

blocks.text: Residential customers and small businesses will receive the “largest reduction in their monthly bills relative to their consumption,” the ERC said.
The order to refund comes after the agency found in its initial review, or “true-up,” that Meralco collected more in distribution charges than its approved rate from January to June this year.
The ERC-approved distribution rate was only P1.3522 per kWh, while Meralco charged P1.5537 per kWh, resulting in excess charges of P0.2015 per kWh, or P5.36 billion more than the approved rate.
The agency said Meralco had proposed refunding the excess charges over 12 months at a rate of P0.0487 per kWh, but the ERC shortened this period to give customers “faster relief.”

“When Meralco collects more than it is entitled to, the ERC will make sure it is returned, and that it is returned quickly. By shortening the refund period to six months, we are giving consumers faster relief at a time when electricity prices remain elevated,” ERC Chairperson Saturnino Juan said in the statement.
The refund will be reflected as a separate line item on customers’ electricity bills labeled “AWAT (Refund)/Collect.”
The ERC noted, however, that the amount is still subject to review and verification during its final evaluation scheduled for October 16 to 23.

articles.title: Remulla asks SC to review doctrine requiring main plunderer, says it shields the guilty
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday urged the Supreme Court (SC) to review the doctrine requiring the identification of a main plunderer in plunder cases, calling it not justice but a shield…

blocks.text: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Monday urged the Supreme Court (SC) to review the doctrine requiring the identification of a main plunderer in plunder cases, calling it not justice but a shield for the guilty.

In his first annual report, Remulla cited Macapagal-Arroyo v. People, where the SC ruled that the prosecution must identify a main plunderer and that the accused personally received or benefited from the act.
“Think about what that means. The smarter the thief. The safer he is. Pass the money through enough dummies, middlemen, and shore companies, and no one can be shown to have touched it,” he said.

“Ang batas laban sa pandarambong ay ginawa para panagutin ang mga nagnanakaw ng mga bilyon-bilyon. Pero sa doktrinang ito, ang pinakamalaking sindikato ang pinakamahirap mahuli. Hindi po ‘yan hustisya. Panangga lang po ‘yan,” he added.
(The law against plunder was created to hold accountable those who steal billions. But under this doctrine, the biggest syndicate is the hardest to catch. That is not justice. It is merely a shield.)
The Ombudsman said that the same scheme was taken advantage of in the flood control controversy.
Remulla said money moved through many hands, and many layers of contractors, and accounts that do not carry the names of those who profited.
He stressed it is time to review and revisit the doctrine.
“Sinasabi ko ito ng may buong paggalang sa Kataas-taasang Hukuman. Panahon na para balikan ang doktrinang ito. It’s time to revisit it,” he said.
(I say this with full respect for the Supreme Court. It is time to revisit this doctrine. It’s time to revisit it.)
Currently, Remulla said his office has filed 39 flood control cases, of which 35 were filed with the Sandiganbayan and four were filed with regional trial courts.

The cases involve 52 individuals, including former Speaker Martin Romualdez, Senator Jinggoy Estrada, former senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, four congressmen, contractors, and Public Works and Highways officials.
Remulla also flagged what he called a “black propaganda” on social media where comment sections are flooded by fake accounts and fake reactions

“‘Wag tayo magpapagamit. ‘Wag tayo magpapauto sa mga taong nagbabayad para sa mga comments o reactions. Kung gusto ninyo malaman ang totoo, 'wag sa comment section kayo tumingin. Tignan ninyo ang mga dokumento, tignan ninyo ang mga kasong naisampa. Tignan ninyo ang mga ebidensya,” he said.

(Let’s not allow ourselves to be used. Let’s not be fooled by people who pay for comments or reactions. If you want to know the truth, don’t look at the comment section. Look at the documents, look at the cases that have been filed. Look at the evidence.)

“To those still hoping that time, money, and connections or a paid army online will save them. They will not. Nasa orte na ang mga kaso and we have done the hardest part. Building them. The next chapter belongs to the courts,” he added.

(To those still hoping that time, money, and connections or a paid army online will save them. They will not. The cases are now in court, and we have done the hardest part. Building them. The next chapter belongs to the courts.)
Meanwhile, he told honest officials to keep serving, assuring they have nothing to fear from the Ombudsman.
“To those who betray public trust, hindi kayo ligtas. Not behind your position, not behind your money, not behind your connections, and not across any border,” he said.
(To those who betray public trust, you are not safe. Not behind your position, not behind your money, not behind your connections, and not across any border.)
“At sa sambayanang Pilipino, ang tanggapang ito ay hindi para sa iisang tao o isang administrasyon. Para ito sa inyo,” he added.
(And to the Filipino people, this office is not for one person or one administration. It is for you.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: 4 Filipinos hurt in Riyadh airport attack, 3 in ICU
articles.summary: Three of the four Filipinos injured in an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remain in intensive care units (ICUs), while the fourth is expected to be discharged,…

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 9:11am
Travellers through stanchion lines at the departure terminal of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on April 2, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Three of the four Filipinos injured in an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remain in intensive care units (ICUs), while the fourth is expected to be discharged, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said Sunday, October 12.
The four Filipinos are recovering at different hospitals in Riyadh, according to the DMW.

"Batay sa ulat ni Labor Attache Dominador Salangga ng Migrant Workers Office (MWO)-Riyadh, tatlo ang kasalukuyang nasa ICU samantalang ang isa pa ay set for discharge from the hospital," the agency said in a statement posted on Facebook.
(Based on a report by Labor Attache Dominador Salangga of the Migrant Workers Office (MWO)-Riyadh, three are currently in the ICU while the other is set for discharge from the hospital.)

The DMW said its teams, along with the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) in Riyadh, are monitoring the condition of the injured Filipinos and providing the necessary assistance and support.
"Wala namang naiulat na Pilipinong nasawi kaugnay ng insidente," the agency said.
(No Filipino deaths have been reported in connection with the incident.)
The MWO is also coordinating with local authorities and hospitals to determine whether other Filipinos were affected by the attack and ensure they receive the necessary assistance.

The DMW advised overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in Saudi Arabia to avoid areas that could be targeted in attacks, including military installations and oil refineries. Those at airports were also told to stay away from crowded areas.
OFWs were urged to follow announcements from the Philippine Embassy, consulates and MWO offices in Saudi Arabia, as well as the social media pages of Saudi government agencies.

Those scheduled to return to the Philippines were advised to contact their airlines before heading to the airport or check the email addresses they used to book their flights for updates. The agency also advised OFWs to ask their employers to regularly check their emails.
The DMW reminded Filipinos not to take photos or videos of attacks or post them on social media, warning that these activities are strictly prohibited in Saudi Arabia and may carry penalties.
Filipinos who need assistance may contact the following offices:

blocks.text: The attack on Saturday, October 10, killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300 others, according to Saudi civil aviation officials. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed the group for the strike, which a diplomatic source attributed to a missile fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
A fresh Houthi strike hit the Riyadh airport on Sunday, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, according to Agence France-Presse.

The fresh attack caused property damage, the extent of which was still being assessed. Authorities extended the airport's closure by 24 hours until 9 p.m. GMT on Monday, or 5 a.m. Tuesday in the Philippines.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump administration to end taxpayer-funded TV ads
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tenn., on Saturday. (Seth Herald/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for ads
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the non-partisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads and called them an illegal misuse of funds.
In granting a temporary restraining order, she told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, Rochon said.

The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment on Sunday night. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

items: Trump administration faces 2 lawsuits for taxpayer-funded ads as midterms draw near
Why pro-Trump ads — paid for with public money — are airing on U.S. TV

blocks.text: The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested they ran afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other federal laws.
The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175-million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump's immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies.

But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential re-election campaign.

articles.title: LIVE: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Oct. 12
articles.summary: The Senate resumes Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Monday, October 12, with the defense panel set to cross-examine forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera.

blocks.text: October 12, 2026 | 8:30am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate resumes Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Monday, October 12, with the defense panel set to cross-examine forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera.

Cabrera, presented by the prosecution as an expert witness, testified on October 9 that Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, had a combined unexplained wealth of P817.87 million from 2022 to 2025.
His findings were based on a review of the couple’s bank and tax records, their business interests’ financial documents and Duterte’s statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALNs).
Cabrera’s report identified P207.7 million in undeclared cash, P143.5 million in undeclared personal and real properties, and P111.85 million in undeclared income attributed to Duterte and Carpio.
The report also cited P142.2 million in undeclared income from Cale 88 Foods Corp. and Metro Chow King Food Corp., as well as P212.63 million in undeclared income from Gencorp Industries Inc.
Cabrera further concluded that Duterte’s SALNs from 2022 to 2025 were untruthful, alleging that substantial assets belonging to the vice president and her spouse were not reported.
He also alleged that Duterte continued participating in various businesses while serving as vice president and that the findings indicated a pattern of constitutional violations.
The defense is expected to challenge Cabrera’s findings as the impeachment trial enters its 38th day.
Watch the continuation of the impeachment trial today at 10 a.m.

articles.title: Imran Khan’s party decries ‘coup’ after Pakistan suspends provincial government
articles.summary:
Suspension of provincial government escalates standoff with Khan’s PTI party a week after his supporters began marching to demand his release

Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a…

blocks.text: Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province ⁠led by Imran ​Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.

President Asif Ali Zardari ​declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.

The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between ⁠Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in ​what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.

Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.

Pakistan’s constitution ‌allows the government to take over from ‌provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number ‌of militant attacks in recent months.

Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.

Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.

Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats ⁠in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say ​the military rigged the vote against him, which the ​military denies.

Cases against Khan range from concerns over state ​gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, ​with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari ​declared the emergency on the advice of ​the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

articles.title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad
articles.summary:
Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary

The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a

blocks.text: The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.
A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports.

“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.

The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.

Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”

“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.

blocks.caption: Firefighters work outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in a mass shooting on Saturday in Erie, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty Images

blocks.text: Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.
after newsletter promotion
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”

Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.

“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.

“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”
“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.

articles.title: Iconic Australian band Powderfinger announce first tour in 17 years
articles.summary: The band, who announced their reunion last week, say they are "absolutely ecstatic" to be playing together again.

blocks.text: Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour – to take place 17 years after they broke up.
The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September.
They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent.
In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again.
"Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said.
"We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play."

"People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all."
The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced.

Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011.
That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets.
Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues.

articles.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
articles.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial (October 12, 2026)
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte continues on Monday, October 12, 2026. Here are the latest news and updates.

blocks.text: The Defense panel on Monday would proceed with the cross-examination of the last witness the House prosecution team has presented in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Once the trial resumes at 10 a.m., Atty. Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst and certified public accountant, is set to return to the witness stand for his cross-examination by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer.
Cabrera on Friday began his testimony regarding allegations on the unexplained wealth of the Vice President under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.
He revealed findings that Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, supposedly had P817.87 million in allegedly undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.
Once the cross-examination of Cabrera finishes, the prosecution and the defense will be given time for the redirect and recross examinations, respectively.
Senator-judges will thereafter be given two minutes each for their interjections.
Bribery charge

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said that presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero is also expected to act on or ask questions regarding the manifestation of the prosecution to drop Article III or the bribery charges in the trial of Duterte.

“Kung sinabi ni Cong. Chel Diokno that they will be resting for Article II and if they will also be dropping Article III, then ang susunod po diyan ay pag-uusapan nila ‘yung ano'ng nangyari sa Article I because they haven't rested on Article I,” Tongol explained in a press conference on Friday.

(If Cong. Chel Diokno said that they would be resting their case on Article II and dropping Article III, then the next step would be to discuss the status of Article I, since they haven't rested their case on it yet.)

“Remember po na magre-rest na po ‘yung lead prosecutor for Article I at that time. However, the presiding officer stopped them because baka possible i-consider the calling of additional witnesses, which is Col. Lachica and Col. Nolasco, I think. At hindi po nag-officially rest pa sila on Article I. Hintayin po natin ano ‘yung gagawin ng House prosecution panel as to that pending article na they haven't rested yet,” he added.

(To recall, the lead prosecutor was supposed to rest the case for Article I, but the presiding officer stopped them because of the possibility of calling additional witnesses — specifically Col. Lachica and Col. Nolasco, I believe. Thus, the prosecution did not officially rest their case on Article I. Let’s wait and see what the House prosecution panel decides regarding that pending Article.)

Article I of the impeachment case accuses Duterte of systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million released to the Department of Education (DepEd) during her tenure as Education Secretary. —Giselle Ombay/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
articles.summary: Many farmers in states that backed the president say they are being hit from all sides, with the crucial midterm elections just weeks away.

blocks.text: Image source, Yvette Mannon
Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports
BySheila Flynn
Senior US Reporter, Nebraska
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.

In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.

On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.

Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.

Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.

Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs

The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.

Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.

Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Lori Potter
Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market - but believes the President

The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.

"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball

blocks.text: "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.

That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.

An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry

blocks.text: Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".

Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"

blocks.text: Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste"
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.

Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.

But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter

blocks.text: Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state

blocks.text: Image source, Lori Potter
Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

articles.title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
articles.summary: After analysing 1,500 videos and images of the Raila Odinga memorial, Africa Eye finds that those killed were far from the scuffles.

blocks.text: Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.

During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."

Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.

The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.

After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.

Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.

Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.

Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia: Second strike kills at least 1 at Riyadh airport
articles.summary: Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam…
articles.byline: Zac Crellin, Matt Ford, Karl Sexton

image.caption: Riyadh airport will be closed until at least Sunday night [FILE: 2019]Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At least one person was killed and 11 others were injured in a stike on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Sunday, a day after a similar attack killed 12 and injured hundreds.
"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.
It later confirmed that the individual killed in the Sunday attack was a Pakistani national.

A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.
The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."
A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport.
Houthis warn airlines after deadly Riyadh airport strike
Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia
The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.

"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.
"We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?
Why are Saudi airports being targeted?

Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.
The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 38: What to expect
articles.summary: The Defense panel on Monday would proceed with the cross-examination of the last witness the House prosecution team has presented in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 12, 2026 6:44am
The Defense panel on Monday would proceed with the cross-examination of the last witness the House prosecution team has presented in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Once the trial resumes at 10 a.m., Atty. Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst and certified public accountant, is set to return to the witness stand for his cross-examination by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer.
Cabrera on Friday began his testimony regarding allegations on the unexplained wealth of the Vice President under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.
He revealed findings that Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, supposedly had P817.87 million in allegedly undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.
Once the cross-examination of Cabrera finishes, the prosecution and the defense will be given time for the redirect and recross examinations, respectively.
Senator-judges will thereafter be given two minutes each for their interjections.
Bribery charge

Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol said that presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero is also expected to act on or ask questions regarding the manifestation of the prosecution to drop Article III or the bribery charges in the trial of Duterte.

“Kung sinabi ni Cong. Chel Diokno that they will be resting for Article II and if they will also be dropping Article III, then ang susunod po diyan ay pag-uusapan nila ‘yung ano'ng nangyari sa Article I because they haven't rested on Article I,” Tongol explained in a press conference on Friday.

(If Cong. Chel Diokno said that they would be resting their case on Article II and dropping Article III, then the next step would be to discuss the status of Article I, since they haven't rested their case on it yet.)

“Remember po na magre-rest na po ‘yung lead prosecutor for Article I at that time. However, the presiding officer stopped them because baka possible i-consider the calling of additional witnesses, which is Col. Lachica and Col. Nolasco, I think. At hindi po nag-officially rest pa sila on Article I. Hintayin po natin ano ‘yung gagawin ng House prosecution panel as to that pending article na they haven't rested yet,” he added.

(To recall, the lead prosecutor was supposed to rest the case for Article I, but the presiding officer stopped them because of the possibility of calling additional witnesses — specifically Col. Lachica and Col. Nolasco, I believe. Thus, the prosecution did not officially rest their case on Article I. Let’s wait and see what the House prosecution panel decides regarding that pending Article.)

Article I of the impeachment case accuses Duterte of systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million released to the Department of Education (DepEd) during her tenure as Education Secretary. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Boy, 13, charged with murder after man stabbed to death in Sydney’s west
articles.summary:
A second boy, 16, was also charged in relation to the stabbing death of a 30-year-old man in Mt Druitt

A thirteen-year-old boy has been charged with murder after a man was stabbed to death…

blocks.text: A thirteen-year-old boy has been charged with murder after a man was stabbed to death in Sydney’s west on Friday.
Emergency services were called to the suburb of Mt Druitt on Friday evening amid reports a man had been assaulted.
Police found the man, aged in his 30s, with stab wounds to his torso.
Paramedics provided assistance to the man, but he died at the scene.
A boy, 13, was arrested on Sunday at Mt Druitt police station and charged with murder, breach of bail and an unrelated offence of robbery.
A second boy, 16, was arrested at a home in Cabramatta later that evening.
He has been charged with murder, accessory after the fact to an offence.
Officials have encouraged anyone with information, including CCTV or dashcam footage, to step forward, saying inquiries continue into the matter.
Supt Brendan Gorman told reporters this weekend detectives were looking into the alleged murder, saying there were about “a dozen people” in the area at the time of the stabbing.
A number of items were seized at the scene, including a bladed instrument.
“At this stage, I would say it’s a horrendous incident and it’s certainly concerning for police,” Gorman said Saturday.
“But again, that will form part of the investigation if it is random, or it is targeted.”
The superintendent added the victim had not been formally identified, but was believed to have “some history” with police.
Both boys were refused bail and will appear before children’s court on Monday.
