articles.title: Disappointed, angry, excited: Albertans weigh in on looming referendum
articles.summary: At a library branch CBC News visited in Calgary, a few people were excited to vote. Others were just starting to follow the process, and several expressed frustration at Alberta even having a…

image.caption: CBC Radio's The Homestretch host Jenny Howe interviewed Calgarian Jim Fedor at the Calgary Public Library’s Seton branch on Thursday. He shared his plans to vote on Oct. 19. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

At a library branch CBC News visited in Calgary, a few people were excited to vote. Others were just starting to follow the process, and several expressed frustration at Alberta even having a referendum.
CBC News heard a lot about unity and unease at a pop-up in a Calgary library
Jim Fedor booked Oct. 19 off work to make sure he can vote in Alberta’s referendum.

“I'm looking forward to it. Never voted in a referendum like this before, so it'll be something new,” said Fedor, who stopped at the CBC News pop-up at the Seton library branch in southeast Calgary last week.

“I'm gonna vote Option 1 on the separation question, for Alberta to stay in Canada, and the other nine questions I plan to vote no for each one,” he said. “I'll get there early, and I'm willing to wait to get in and vote.”
“I think it's important for everyone to have their voices heard. A lot of places in the world don't allow voting on much of anything. So I feel quite lucky to be able to vote and make my vote count.”

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: CBC News set up at the library to get a sense of how Albertans are feeling as the referendum campaigns head into their final week. We set out Post-It notes and markers, and invited patrons to share their thoughts on the question: What are you thinking about as you get ready to vote?
Library patrons left their thoughts at a CBC News pop-up in the Calgary Public Library's Seton branch. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Parents came by with their kids; high school students stopped in after their classes ended; seniors swung by to pick up books on hold. A low hum filled the busy building.
Some Albertans frustrated at the vote

A few people were excited to vote, like Fedor. Others were just starting to follow the process and had not yet decided how they would cast their ballots; several expressed frustration at even having the vote.

items: 'People are overwhelmed': Community groups rally to inform voters ahead of Alberta referendum
Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll

blocks.text: That’s how Christine Nelson was feeling.

“I'm really disappointed. The majority of people do not want to separate, and we have to spend taxpayers’ money to vote on something that's not going to go through unless there's some kind of, you know, crookedness going on. It's ridiculous,” said Nelson.
Charmaine Coutinho, who stopped by with her young daughter, had a similar sentiment.

“I am feeling anger about the increase in racism and otherness caused by legitimizing these extreme perspectives through government actions,” she said. “I am saying no to everything, and we are, and I am, very much in favour of staying in Canada.”

From left to right, Michael Chudleigh, Charmaine Coutinho and her daughter, and Christine Nelson. They all stopped by to share their thoughts at the CBC News pop-up in Seton on Thursday. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Michael Chudleigh said he is voting the same, but trying to stay open to difference.
“I'm trying not to be angry about the whole thing and understand that those who disagree with me have their reasons, even if I can't see them.”
Friends at odds over separation
One pair of seniors were laughing and chatting as they stopped by on their way for coffee. The two women said they are good friends, who meet regularly.
One is passionate about staying in Canada, while the other is casting her vote to explore leaving.

They don’t talk about the referendum. “We might not be friends after!” said the pro-unity friend. She didn’t want to be interviewed, but earlier said her father fought for Canada and she’d never want to see it splintered.

The other friend came back later to write her thoughts on the whiteboard: “I think the Oct. 19 [referendum] is more like a memorandum of understanding thing and gets people talking and looking into our rights and fairness/democracy. But many people have been led to be afraid it’s a final say or referendum to leave their country or be taken over by Trump!”
She wrote that separatists fear the way Ottawa has been asserting control over individuals, such as freezing bank accounts during the trucker convoy.

items: First came the blockade. Then came separatism. Old tensions revived in Coutts
How anti-COVID activism injected life into Alberta's separatist movement

blocks.text: Newcomers express love for Canada
As the afternoon wore on, our board filled with messages, with a lot of love for Canada.
“I love Canada; I’ll vote to stay here,” wrote one person.
“I love Canada, this is my home,” wrote another.

David Aldana immigrated from Colombia and has been following the referendum campaigns, even though he can't vote. Other Albertans with permanent residency but no Canadian citizenship also left messages on the board. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Several people with permanent residency but not Canadian citizenship stopped by. One was David Aldana, who moved to Canada from Colombia.

“If I could vote, I would stay with Canada, and because I feel that unity is better,” he said. “I think unity is better for the country itself. I'm in love with Canada. I'm in love with the freedom that we have here.”
Concerns the vote could backfire
In Alberta, support for independence had been polling at about 27 per cent this spring, according to a poll from Janet Brown Opinion Research commissioned by CBC News.

That softened to 23 per cent in a similar poll by Janet Brown in September, which also found Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party lost some support, likely due to frustration over the vote.

One man at the library called it a nightmare. He wrote: “Talk about backfiring. Rather than more consideration from Ottawa we are now facing a potential NDP resurgence (the worst outcome you could imagine).”

On the left, a Ukrainian newcomer left her concerns: the referendum reminds her of separation votes in the Ukrainian regions of Crimea and Donbas. On the right, a public servant wrote a note about his hope for a transparent referendum process. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who stopped by after class at the nearby Joane Cardinal-Schubert High School. He said at school they tried to look at the separation arguments from both sides.

“Surprisingly, a lot of my class wanted to stay. And I really found that fascinating ‘cause there's just one of my friends who is heavily right. He always agrees with whatever right-wingers say but this time … he wants to stay in Canada,” Asher said.
“It kind of just shows that as a country — it sounds a bit corny, but there's a lot of love and unity. I think that's really special, and I think we just can't give that up.”
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who discussed the Alberta referendum question at school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
'Strong opinions on both sides'
The voices for unity were loudest and most common at the library Thursday. But it’s one location, on one afternoon.

items: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favours separation as party stares down ‘tough days’ ahead
Fight for independence won't end after referendum: Alberta Prosperity Project leader

blocks.text: Destiny Fox stopped by and suggested you can’t judge how people in general are feeling by those most willing to speak up.

“I don't think that a lot of people are being very open about their opinion to leave Canada as honestly as people who want to stay in Canada,” Fox said. “So you're just not hearing as much … You're not going to see the lawn signs on people's personal property because they don't want to get into it with their neighbours. But I think that there are a lot of strong opinions on both sides.

“I'm glad that we're having this referendum because I feel like it's giving everybody an opportunity to voice their feelings. And I don't necessarily feel that I want to separate from Canada, but I do want the premier to have the power to go back to Ottawa and say this is how Albertans are feeling.”
Turning Alberta referendum polling data into art
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Elise Stolte runs project-based engagement efforts for the CBC Calgary newsroom. She has 20 years of experience telling the stories of her community and has been recognized for feature writing, social impact and community-based journalism. You can reach her at elise.stolte@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Poland arrests man over plot to kill PM Donald Tusk
articles.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed the arrest hours after police received information about a possible assassination plot. Poland is still reeling from a wave of school violence this week.

image.caption: Amid a spate of violence this week, Tusk said 'spontaneous' attacks were 'inspired by online activity' [FILE: October 8]Image: Albert Zawada/PAP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland on Sunday detained a man accused of plotting to assassinate Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the country's defense minister, the PM wrote on X.
"The man threatening an attack has been detained," Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their "swift and decisive action."
The Interior Minister also confirmed the arrest. No details about the man's identity were made public.
Security chiefs convene urgent talks

Tusk's tweet followed an emergency meeting by Poland's security services to discuss what officials said was a potential attack against both the prime minister and Defense ‌Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
The meeting was convened at short notice after police received a tip-off about a possible assassination attempt, a spokesperson for the Interior Ministry wrote in a post on X.
While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, Poland remains on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.
What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?
Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.

The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.

A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.
On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.

Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.
Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.
What did Tusk say about the school attacks?
On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.
"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.

The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."
Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."
The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.

Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

articles.title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
articles.summary: A flash flood at the Budhi Gandaki River has swept away several buildings and bridges, two months after catastrophic floods hit the country.

blocks.text: A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal.
The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed.
It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.
Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.

Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

articles.title: Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
articles.summary: President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his party.

image.caption: Authorities have set up massive roadblocks across Pakistan to keep Khan supporters at bayImage: Abdul Majeed/AFP

blocks.text: Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.
Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.
The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.
Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.
Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Last Sunday, thousands of Imran Khan supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital Islamabad, with organizers declaring their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.
Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, left office in April 2022, when he lost a no-confidence vote.
He has been in prison since August 2023.
Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023.
Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks.
The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

articles.title: Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
articles.summary: The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any…

image.caption: A car is covered in rubble from houses damaged by an earthquake in Villa de los Santos, Panama, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any deaths to the quakes but reported damages in all 10 of Panama's provinces and two Indigenous territories.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos

The 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes on Friday toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometres southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometres.

items: Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama

blocks.text: Presidential Minister Juan Carlos Orillac announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, told reporters the state had reports of 27 people with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Hundreds of homes were damaged
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

The Civil Protection agency tallied roughly 420 homes and about the same number of public schools damaged. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64 kilometres northeast of the epicenter, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government's guidance on what to do next.
Canadian in Panama experiences aftershock live on air | Hanomansing Live

"We've been here since 1 p.m. yesterday; we haven't moved," Tony Jimenez, whose home partially collapsed, said while sitting with relatives under a tent. "It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense -- truly intense."
The collapsed Church of San Atanasio was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a Latin American region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months.

Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people.

The notably lower toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Rising sea levels prompt evacuations
Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

On Isla Cana, off the Pacific coast of Los Santos, approximately 300 people were evacuated because of rising sea levels and rough surf. Meanwhile, in the city of Penonome, around 150 kilometres from the capital, a shelter was housing 13 people, including five children. The earthquakes caused a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
In Panama City, one of the water treatment plants supplying the area operated at 20 per cent capacity on Saturday, and tent facilities with cots were set up at six hospitals.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday but reopened hours later.
Powerful earthquake hits Panama, triggers tsunami warnings

But hundreds of travelers on major Panama-based airlines like Copa Airlines were left stranded in airports around the region. Their connections through Tocumen — one of the biggest travel hubs in the region — were canceled or delayed. In Mexico City's airport, airline employees scrambled as families with babies were sleeping on the floor Saturday while one woman from Venezuela shouted in panic that the flight through Panama was one of the only ways she could return home to Caracas.

The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.

The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region.
A vehicle lies crushed beneath a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Penonome, Panama, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.
Countries offer help

Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The U.S. Department of State on Saturday said it mobilized a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments.
The U.S. government also pledged $5 million for humanitarian assistance.
U.S. Southern Command also said two helicopters supported by the State Department's drug-control bureau had delivered 2,000 pounds of food to Panamanian communities affected by the earthquakes.

articles.summary: Germany's foreign minister has said Berlin is behind Ukraine's president and will keep pressuring Russia to end its war. Meanwhile, Deutsche Bank's CEO warned that political extremism is spooking…

blocks.text: October 11, 2026
Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors
Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.

Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."

The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction ‌between a state government and Germany as a whole," he ‌said.
"It's ​seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."
Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.
The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.
"Whether ​it's Saxony-Anhalt with ⁠the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. ⁠And it's anything ​but investment-friendly."

Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."

The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers…

items: 15m agoHouthis issue warning against use of Saudi airports
18m ago12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike
20m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Houthis issue warning against use of Saudi airports
The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers and airlines against using Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack.
It’s the first public message from the group since Saturday’s deadly assault.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said airports and airspace “are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces”, he said, adding that the group was pursuing: “airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation”.
He said the airports in Mecca and Medina – the holiest cities in Islam- were excepted.
All week the Houthis have been striking the main international airport, which was first targeted about a fortnight ago as fighting ramped up within Yemen.

The Saudi-led coalition backing the government forces in Yemen have launched an outright offensive in the country this week to try and push back the Houthis who’ve rapidly seized and gained territory these past weeks.

The Houthis have taken over islands in the Bab al- Mandab strait and also staked stronger positions along the Red Sea, crucially seizing control of the main passageway through which its enemy state – top oil exporter Saudi Arabia- had been diverting its flows as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut off.
12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike

Saturday’s attack was the third launched on the Saudi capital’s main airport this week- with the missile making it past Saudi air defences to strike terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid airport where hundreds of passengers were awaiting domestic flights.
The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 309 at last count, say Saudi officials.
The dead include four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis.
The Dammam airport has been an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of rapidly unfolding events in the Middle East.

After attacking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport on Saturday in strikes which killed at least 12 people and injured 309, the Houthis have issued another message this morning about the kingdom’s airports.

In response to the Houthi’s assault – the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in over a decade – US President Donald Trump has said Washington may join the Saudis in carrying out air strikes against the Iran-backed group in Yemen.
Trump said: “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

articles.title: What happens when a Google data centre comes to town? Southern India is finding out
articles.summary: India is vying to secure a piece of the AI boom, and letting Google clear hundreds of acres to build a $15 billion US data centre hub near its eastern coast. It will be the company's largest such…

image.caption: Engineering student Bali Chararan Teja, front, thought he would inherit his family's farmland — which will now be part of an AI data centre Google is building in and around Visakhapatnam, India. (Kate Kyle/CBC)

blocks.text: A group of farmers sits under the shade of a Jamun tree, chewing over the big news in their village: Google is moving in.
Google, with India's powerful Adani Group, is building a massive $15 billion US AI data centre hub in and around Visakhapatnam, a port city on India's east coast.
Farmer Bali Narasingha Rao owned one acre in Tarluvada. Pressured to sell, he says he got 17 lakhs, about $25,000, for his land — but he's unsettled about the future.
Earth movers are clearing more than 260 acres here — the biggest of three sites.
"Our land is gone, and that land was our livelihood," he said, adding that some of the village leaders told them the data centre was locating here because other countries didn’t want it.
All of a sudden his rural village is part of the AI boom.
In the race to secure a piece of it, the state government of Andhra Pradesh, has welcomed Google's five-year, multi-billion dollar investment, covering over 600 acres on three sites.
See the scale of Google's construction

At the ground-breaking ceremony in April, N. Chandrababu Naidu, the state's chief minister, said "Google is very important. If they are willing to come I'll do everything I can to extend co-operation."

The build out in this corner of India for a one-gigawatt hub is the largest for Google outside the U.S. and in many ways mirrors some concerns in other jurisdictions over water use, energy demands and noise from data centres.
"Having AI data centres is something I think India must do," said Sribharat Mathukumilli the MP for Vishakhapatnam, adding the state has big plans to attract fintech companies, banks and AI startups.
"So this is an ecosystem play. It is not a singular play."
But there is opposition from some environmental and human rights advocates, who argue the project's approvals were fast-tracked and that the costs outweigh the rewards.
Sribharat Mathukumilli, the MP for Vishakhapatnam, promotes the economic benefits of attracting data centres to India. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"This data centre boom for us doesn't look more than a real estate project," said 26-year-old Deeksha Vanguru, a community organizer originally from Vizag, as Visakhapatnam is known.
"It is just whoever can secure the most amount of land, and slap a bunch of concrete there."
The "Stop Dirty Data Centres" campaign regularly canvasses villagers and neighbourhoods next to the three construction sites which make up Google's AI hub.
Recently Meta blocked the campaign's Instagram account under India's information technology rules.
India, Vanguru says, is fertile ground for big tech companies to expand.
"We have weak laws in terms of environmental laws, regulation laws and we give out a lot of subsidies," she said.
A municipal reservoir in Visakhapatnam shows the effects of this year's drought and weak monsoon. (Saraskanth TK/CBC)
'Huge economic value'
To attract Google, the state offered discounts on land and concessions on water and electricity tariffs for ten years.
"This is of huge economic value," said Mathukumilli, the MP. "Over time, while [Google] may have some incentives upfront, it will be a long-term economic boost."
Vanguru sees it differently.

"The central government has categorized data centres as essential infrastructures. In a country where schools are in a bad shape, where hospitals are not available," she said. "Fix the bottom foundation first."

Google's project, according to the government, could create up to 150,000 indirect jobs in related tech industries, and 4,000 a year during construction. But running the data centres will require only hundreds of permanent employees; many of those will be service jobs to maintain the facilities, argue opponents.
Demonstrators march against the Google hub in Visakhapatnam, on Sept. 19. Activists regularly canvass villagers and neighbourhoods next to the three construction sites. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
'Completely unhappy'
In the rural village of Tarluvada, just outside Visakhapatnam, a group of young men approach CBC News.
"We‘re talking [for] our village members, ma'am,” said 23-year-old Bali Charan Teja. ”We are completely unhappy with the data centre."

Local farmer Bali Narasingha Rao, left, was persuaded to sell his one acre of land for the data centre. It was the only land he'd ever owned and now he worries about the next generation. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"It's a data storage centre, useful for only storage or cooling of the systems so I can't believe that we can get any employment here."
He's studying to be a civil engineer and thought he would inherit his family's farm land — now sold off — as part of his legacy.
Nearby in Vizag, some residents are worried the data centre will use up too much water.
A weak monsoon and drought this year have stretched water resources. The local reservoir has receded and ground water is dropping.
Area resident V. Jyothi says she welcomes the potential new jobs, but worries about the water shortages already plaguing her part of Visakhapatnam. (Kate Kyle/CBC)
"The water problem has become very serious," said V. Jyothi, standing in front of her modest two-room home.
"We know that the data centre is coming, and we have heard that it could lead to water problems."
Air cooling system
The state government says water will not be diverted from residential use, but people are skeptical.

Google, in an email statement to CBC News, says it will use an "advanced air cooling system," in place of water cooling, "limiting water consumption​" to primarily restrooms and kitchens. It says the facility is designed to keep "boundary sound" outside the data centre "below 55 decibels … roughly the volume of a dishwasher."

A court challenge in August failed to halt work on the data centre hub, parts of which are scheduled to be operational in 2028. Google is also laying three subsea cables for data connectivity off the Visakhapatnam coast.

On the beach Sudeep Pillarisetty, a software developer and entrepreneur, is excited that Google chose his city for a data centre, confident it will kick off data science and engineering roles for young tech professionals.

blocks.text: "I hope Google provides a subsidy for any of the Indian startups to create their own AI models — made in India," he said.
But in the village on the bench under the tree, the farmers are still debating the merits.
"This land is the only livelihood and security we have for our children, " said Bali Sanyasa Rao.
"We will know whether it is beneficial or harmful only after the data centre is completed."

articles.title: 'You're Russian now': Ukrainians raised in Crimea share how Russia trained them to become future soldiers
articles.summary: Three Ukrainians who grew up in occupied Crimea describe how Russia trained them to become future soldiers for its war on Ukraine, including school classes on how to handle weapons — part of a larger…
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Terence McKenna, Alex Shprintsen

image.caption: From left, Ukrainians Daria Tomashova, Matvii Chos and Daria Fursova grew up in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they describe being subjected to indoctrination and forced to do military training. They have each shared their experiences with the international community at conferences and the United Na

blocks.text: Growing up in Crimea under Russian occupation, Matvii Chos feared he would be drafted into the Russian army as soon as he became an adult.

"If you're a man and you turn 18 years old, they almost immediately draft you," said Chos, 19, who enrolled at a Moscow university to avoid conscription and later escaped Russia with the help of a Ukrainian non-profit.

But he says the brainwashing and militarization started much earlier. Chos says they began having special cadet classes in 2020, when he was a sixth-grade student. They were trained in a range of military techniques — loading and reloading weapons, marching, tactical medicine — a co-ordinated effort, Chos says, to create future soldiers to fight his fellow Ukrainians.
"What Russia is doing is occupying territories, kidnapping children and turning them [into] Russian soldiers," he said.
Russia kidnapping, brainwashing children to be future soldiers, says Ukrainian teen

Fifty countries signed a pledge at the Pathways to Peace international conference held in Toronto on Sept. 29, expressing concern about the militarization of children in occupied territories and calling for the “immediate, safe and unconditional return” of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred into Russia.

The indoctrination and forced military training Chos was subjected to is an experience shared by many Ukrainian youth in territories controlled by Russia — an issue especially urgent, human rights experts say, because of how vulnerable children are.
"Childhood has an expiration date," said Oleksandra Matviichuk, a Ukrainian human rights lawyer who heads the Center for Civil Liberties, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.
"The children from occupied territories, they're losing their childhood. We lose these children."
Speaking Ukrainian forbidden
Other young Ukrainians who spoke to CBC News outlined the various ways Russian culture and values were imposed on them as children.
Daria Fursova, 23, remembers how quickly her elementary school curriculum changed after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 when she was 11.
"The administration said that there will no longer be Ukrainian books in school, in classes," she said, recalling the start of fifth grade.
How Russia justifies its invasion of Ukraine to children in occupied Crimea
Not long after, Fursova’s school stopped teaching Ukrainian and instead began instructing them in Russian history and the Russian language.

Speaking Ukrainian and Crimean Tatar — a language considered "highly endangered" by UNESCO — was forbidden, even during breaks, according to 18-year-old Daria Tomashova, who says the indoctrination was "everywhere," from textbooks in school to what was broadcast on TV.
Chos has similar memories of the sudden shift after the occupation.
"We started to learn [the] Russian anthem at school, learn Russian songs, learn Russian poems," he said. "They said to us, 'You're Russian now. You lived all of your life in Russia.' "

Fursova left Crimea to study in Kyiv in 2021 before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but says the situation in Crimea has since become "way worse." Her old school posted lessons on social media defending the war, and she says many of her former classmates have since joined the Russian army.
Daria Fursova, 23, shares her experience growing up in occupied Crimea at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 23, during the sixth summit of the Crimea Platform. (UN Web TV)
20,000 children abducted

Beyond the Russification of occupied Crimea, the international community has raised particular concern with how Russia has forcibly separated tens of thousands of Ukrainian children from their families and taken them into Russian territory — an act Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as "mass kidnapping" amounting to genocide.

Many of those children have shared stories of abuse while in Russian custody, including being placed in isolation cells for not being co-operative in Russian re-education camps. Other children are given new identities, naturalized as Russian citizens and forcibly adopted into foster families in Russia.
The children abducted by Putin’s war machine
Ukrainian officials estimate that Russia has unlawfully deported 20,000 children since the invasion began in February 2022. Of those, only about 2,650 have been returned so far.
The co-ordinated campaign has led to charges at the International Criminal Court against Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova.

items: Ukrainian children abducted by Russia appeal for help from Canadian MPs

blocks.text: Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand says she holds Putin personally responsible for the policies that have led to Ukrainian children being "stolen" from their families.

"My hope is that we ensure the full return of all Ukrainian children, and every single person who has committed an injustice in stealing these children face the consequences that international law requires," Anand said in an interview with CBC.
Canada committed to bringing Ukrainian children home: Anand
Children just want to return to 'normal life'

Anand says Canada has committed nearly $7 million to support organizations that work to bring Ukrainian children home and fund psychological support for the trauma endured as a result of the "indoctrination, militarization and essentially the Russian attempt to convert these Ukrainian children into members of Russia’s war machine."
One of those organizations is Save Ukraine, a charity that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to rescue them.

Its founder, Mykola Kuleba, says he is grateful for Canada’s leadership on the issue, but emphasized how critical the present situation is, with some young Ukrainians now presumably fighting as Russian soldiers and dying on the battlefield.
'Long way' to justice and accountability for abducted Ukrainian kids, says NGO founder

"We should understand that we're running out of time for these children, and we're losing every day someone who's taken forcibly to the Russian army," said Kuleba, the former commissioner for children’s rights in Ukraine.
Kuleba says the children they bring home tell him they just want to live in peace with their families in their hometowns.
"They want [to] survive. They want to return to a normal life. They want to stay with their loved ones."

items: 'We need strong support': Ukraine fighting to bring children back from Russia
There can be no peace with Russia until Ukrainian children come home, says advocate

blocks.text: Chos was eventually able to escape Russia with the help of Save Ukraine, which gave him food, shelter, mental health support and documentation.

But the process was nerve-racking: Chos had to travel to the Ukrainian consulate in Belarus twice, and said if Russian authorities had searched him and found anything suggesting he was pro-Ukraine, he would be facing over a decade in Russian prison.

Chos, left, and Tomashova speak at the Pathways to Peace international conference in Toronto on Sept. 28. The Ukrainian couple fell in love and married after being rescued by Save Ukraine, a non-profit that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to get them to safety. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)
Now a married couple, Chos and Tomashova shared their experiences at the recent international conference in Toronto.
"I managed to escape," Chos told the room of delegates, "but a lot of children are still left there."

articles.title: Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in Peru
articles.summary:
Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’

  • Get our

blocks.text: An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.
Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.

“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.
“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.
“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”

The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.

His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

articles.title: Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?
articles.summary: Georgia became a hub for surrogate pregnancies after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. DW spoke with parents, and those who wanted to become parents, about the hidden costs of a…

image.caption: After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, much of the surrogacy industry shifted to GeorgiaImage: SWR

blocks.text: Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts.

Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia. That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia. So, Olga and Daniel traveled there.
Georgia the new destination for surrogate mothers

In the past years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. And since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023.

Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment.
Surrogacy in the US: a different path to parenthood

Anastasia says she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.

"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She says she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.

Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.
Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.
Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand

Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."

Both work in the medical field, and Olga says perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she says. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga adds.

In the spring of 2024, the married couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.

"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel tell DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."
Human rights experts criticize legislation

Georgian laws have a weak spot, the human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze tells DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents, and the clinics, but they do not consider the roles that agencies play.

In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.
Surrogacy laws and rules vary widely across Africa

After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program, or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.
Agencies guided by material interests

"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya from the University of Leeds tell DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."

Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," Olga says.

And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga recounts. "I felt like I was being manipulated."
The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.
Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.

articles.title: Germany's population is shrinking, but not everywhere
articles.summary: By 2045, Germany will have more older people, fewer workers and a smaller population overall. Yet some regions will defy this trend. Their success depends on how much they have to offer.

image.caption: Some areas in Germany will see population numbers dwindleImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's population is expected to decline from 83.5 million in 2025 to around 81.8 million by 2045, according to a new study from the Berlin Institute for Population and Development (Berlin-Institut für Bevölkerung und Entwicklung), in collaboration with the Wüstenrot Foundation, a non-profit that supports research on housing, urban development, and social change.

The decline in population alone is not the central challenge. More significant is the continuing rise in the number of retirees alongside a steadily shrinking workforce. Across Germany, the working-age population is projected to decrease by 4.7% by 2045.

"The baby boomer generation is retiring, while significantly smaller cohorts are following. Birth rates are falling, and immigration is not sufficient to offset the growing surplus of deaths over births," said Institute President Catherina Hinz when presenting the study in Berlin.
The term "baby boomers" refers to those born in the 1960s, when annual births exceeded one million. Thereafter, the birth rate fell sharply, effectively halving.
The economy matters

Germany's population may be shrinking, but according to the study, this trend is far from uniform across the country. In the years ahead, a region's economic attractiveness, and the financial strength that comes with it, will become even more important than it is today.

"Some regions will lose substantial numbers of residents and workers in the years ahead, while others continue to grow. Even within eastern Germany, southern Germany, and rural areas, the demographic and economic divide is widening," said Hinz.

"Demographic change is unfolding before our very eyes, and its effects are being felt across the country," Hinz added. "Its consequences can still be mitigated, but they can no longer be avoided. And the longer we wait, the narrower our scope for action will become."

Hinz's warning is echoed by Frederick Sixtus of the Berlin Institute. Almost every region now records more deaths than births, he notes, a consequence of decades of low birth rates. The implication is clear: Migration, both inward and outward, now shapes a region's demographic trajectory. Over recent decades, immigration from abroad has repeatedly helped stabilize population trends. Yet migration alone is no longer enough to halt the aging of society.

According to the study, several factors are critical if a region is to remain attractive to people relocating from abroad or from other parts of Germany: High-quality jobs offering good pay and working conditions, a sufficient supply of skilled workers for local businesses, financially robust municipalities, reliable childcare, and efficient transport and mobility infrastructure.
Berlin leads the way

Many major cities are expected to continue to grow in the years ahead, according to Manuel Slupina of the Wüstenrot Foundation. The study projects that Berlin will lead the way, with the capital's population increasing by almost 10% by 2045. Other cities expected to attract people include Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Munich, and Düsseldorf in western Germany, as well as Leipzig, Dresden, and Potsdam in the east.

The study's authors argue that the familiar distinction between urban and rural areas does not hold true everywhere. The hinterlands of many major cities are also expected to grow. While young people are increasingly drawn to metropolitan centers, families with children tend to settle in the surrounding areas. Among the places likely to lose population are several large cities in western Germany, including Bremen, Duisburg, Dortmund, and Kaiserslautern, whose economic appeal has gradually diminished. At the bottom of the ranking are many sparsely populated regions, a large number of them in eastern Germany.
Competition for talent

Twelve of the 20 districts and independent cities with the weakest overall ratings are now located in eastern Germany, up from five in the previous assessment in 2019. According to the study, these regions are also expected to see the steepest declines in their working-age populations, with losses of up to 18% by 2045. The authors conclude that competition for workers is therefore set to become one of the key demographic challenges of the decades ahead.

In this competition, the southern German states of Bavariaand Baden-Württemberg are regarded as having the strongest prospects. Bavaria ranks particularly highly thanks to its robust economy, which is thriving across much of the state, and its strong labor market. Women, older people, and people without German citizenship are also more likely to be employed in Bavaria than elsewhere. The ranking shows that economically successful regions are more effective at integrating different population groups into the labor market than weaker ones.
Why Germans want children but are having fewer babies
Policymakers must find local solutions
Under Germany's constitution, the country is committed to ensuring that people enjoy comparable opportunities, and with them the prospect of a good life, regardless of where they live.

The researchers offer clear recommendations to policymakers. They argue that the focus must be on addressing structural challenges and regional disparities. "What may be the right response for a growing major city is not necessarily the right one for a shrinking rural district," says Slupina. Tailor-made solutions are needed, but they require the right framework conditions. "There needs to be less rigid regulation, more scope for local initiative, and greater financial resources, especially for municipalities and those actively engaged at the local level." Slupina's message is clear: Regions should be trusted to shape their own futures.

Local authorities would no doubt welcome that. For years, mayors and district administrators have been calling for greater financial autonomy. They are currently seeking a larger share of overall tax revenues for municipalities. The federal government and the states, however, argue that they face budgetary constraints of their own. Yet both sides recognize that, sooner or later, Germany will have little choice but to reform its system of fiscal federalism.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
articles.summary:
More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations

Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as…

blocks.text: Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.

The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).

blocks.caption: A car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters

blocks.text: The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.

About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.

In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.

“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”

blocks.caption: Elodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday.  Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPA

blocks.text: Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.

That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.

Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.

The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.

articles.title: India's 'Cockroach' movement leaders say 'the fight has just begun' after a large protest in Delhi
articles.summary: Leaders of the youth-led protest movement demanding India's election commissioner step down say the "fight has just begun" after they were released from detention following a large demonstration in…

image.caption: Parts of Delhi were locked down Saturday with a mammoth deployment of police and paramilitary personnel,Image: Abiraj Kumar Arulgnanakumar/DW

blocks.text: October 11, 2026
CJP issues fresh appeal for peaceful protests
CJP co-convenor Saurav Das called on people from across India to again protest in a peaceful manner.
"This demonstration is still on," Das said as he spoke about reported protester detentions taking place for a second day.

"We are not going to move back, we appeal to all Indian citizens that you will have to fight. You will have to come out on the streets. Wherever you are, you will have to do a peaceful demonstration," he told a press conference.

"This system cannot go on like this. This system is broken. This system is corrupt… and this system only works in the service of two people," Das said, going on to name Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah.
The CJP's Ashutosh Ranka said peaceful protesters who wanted to demonstrate at a designated protest site were picked up.
"The fight has just begun…Modi and Shah should feel ashamed for treating this fight like a war," he said.
Indian authorities try to shut down a 'Cockroach' protest

articles.title: US: Justice Department probes Trump's press pool boycott for antitrust violation
articles.summary: The Department of Justice is investigating whether the five news organizations violated antitrust laws when they suspended their coverage of Trump in protest. The networks under probe are ABC, CBS,…

image.caption: Trump has long been at odds with the mainstream media, regularly calling them 'fake news' [FILE: September 2026]Image: Alex Wroblewski/AFP

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice announced on Saturday that it is investigating whether the White House press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month, violated the nation's anti trust law.
Group boycotts among business competitors might violate US law, spokesperson Emily Covington said.
"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said.
The networks under the scrutiny are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate.
"The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access," Zamora said on X. "The public's right to know depends on that access."
Under pressure — Trump's fractured America
Why is Trump's press pool under investigation?

On September 21, a pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage after the Trump administration barred news networks CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying covering the president was a "privilege, not a right."
Trump bans media outlets from White House
As a result, the five television networks suspended coverage in protest and refused to provide replacement program.

The news outlets also sued the administration, accusing it of violating free speech and free press rights under the First Amendment of the US Constitution and pursuing retaliation over their coverage.
On September 24, the White House reinstated their press credentials after a US district Judge ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate and restore" their access.
The president has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and clashed with reporters during interviews.
The White House press pool is a roating group of news outlets which cover the president and accompany him on official duties.

CNN is one of the five news organizations, along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBS, that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the cost of covering the president and take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
The White House press pool has now become a proxy for a fight over press freedom.
Trump vs. the press: Who controls the story?

articles.title: Saudi Arabia extends airport closure and moves Riyadh schools online after deadly strike

image.caption: People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia on Sunday kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online as Yemen's Houthi rebels threatened new strikes across the kingdom, a day after a missile attack killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.

Saturday's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran's-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he was considering whether to join Saudi strikes against the rebels, a scenario that could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through a crucial waterway and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.

Later Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry reported that a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

items: Saudi-led coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport

blocks.text: The ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said that 60 per cent of those killed were women and children.
Riyadh shutters airport, schools as Houthis threaten more strikes

The kingdom said Sunday that schools in the capital would hold classes online until the end of the week. Meanwhile, authorities extended an ongoing airport closure until at least 9 p.m. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
While the Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for Saturday's attack, they have acknowledged targeting Saudi airports and oil installations in the past.
Another deadly strike on Saudi airport as Houthis escalate attacks

Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the group's military spokesperson, warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces." He wrote on the social media platform X that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina were exempt.

The latest attack on the Saudi airport drew condemnations from Arab countries, including Iraq, Lebanon and Syria, as well as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
"Attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence," von der Leyen wrote Sunday on X. "They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes."
Details surface about airport fatalities

The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56 years old, from Syria's northern Idlib province, and had left during the country's civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed in the attack on the airport, her niece said.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom.

Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
People gather outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid airport in Riyadh on Saturday. (The Associated Press)

A U.S. attack would deepen American involvement in an unpopular regional war that has threatened Trump's Republican party in upcoming U.S. midterm elections. Both Trump and Iran insist the American election calendar has no effect on their decisions on how to end the seven-month-old conflict.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The airport has no military facilities.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
Iran can use Houthis to pressure key U.S. ally
The latest fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis comes as negotiations between Iran and the U.S. aimed at ending their war appear to be at a standstill.

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. Houthi attacks, along with their control of the Bab el-Mandeb waterway, also threaten to add new disruptions to the flow of oil from the region.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July, when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.

Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

articles.title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
articles.summary: Film-maker Sue Kim talks about having unprecedented access to K-Pop idol Lisa Manobal at her most candid.

blocks.text: What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".

In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.

That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.

"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."

Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
